sentences: In many French villages, small businesses are closing one after another.
The bakery, the grocery store, the café: once at the heart of local life, they are gradually disappearing.
The reasons are well known.
Supermarkets, often located outside of towns, offer lower prices.
In addition, online shopping allows people to order everything without leaving their homes.
One might think it's just a simple economic problem.
However, the issue is deeper.
When the last bakery closes, it's not just a store that disappears.
It's a place where residents used to meet, talk, and know each other.
Some municipalities are reacting.
They help shopkeepers set up, or open stores managed by the village itself.
Nothing guarantees that these efforts will be enough.
But they at least show that many refuse to watch their town center die without taking action.

sentences: People often think that only one language is spoken in France: French.
In reality, the country has many regional languages, such as Breton, Occitan, Corsican, or Alsatian.
For a long time, these languages were discouraged, especially in schools.
Children were asked to speak only French, and many families stopped passing down their grandparents' language.
As a result, today, most of these languages are fragile.
Some are only spoken by elderly people and are at risk of disappearing in the coming decades.
However, an opposite movement exists.
Some schools offer instruction in these languages, and young parents choose to enroll their children in them.
Singers and writers keep them alive in different ways.
Saving a language is never easy, as it's not enough to study it: it must be spoken daily.
But as long as people care about it, nothing is really lost.

sentences: The objection arises with every spectacular launch, with every announcement of a mission to Mars, and it has the force of obviousness: how can we justify spending fortunes on space exploration when so many problems remain unsolved on Earth?
Hunger, poverty, illness, climate: the list of urgent issues on Earth is long, and spending billions to send robots to contemplate distant rocks may seem, at best, a whim, and at worst, an indecency.
The argument deserves to be taken seriously — and it is by taking it seriously that we discover it is weaker than it appears.
The first response, the most down-to-earth: space exploration is not money thrown into the void.
A considerable part of the technologies that equip our daily lives has originated, directly or indirectly, from space research.

The weather forecasts that save lives, the location systems that guide our movements, a host of advances in medicine, materials, and miniaturized electronics: all these applications stem from the efforts made to go into space.
The history of technology teaches a constant lesson: fundamental research, seemingly useless, almost always leads to unforeseen and valuable applications.
Giving up exploration in the name of immediate utility means depriving ourselves of future utilities that we cannot foresee.
The second response, less expected: space teaches us to know Earth.

It is from space that we monitor the climate, the state of forests, the melting of ice, the health of oceans; without satellites, our understanding of climate change — this very urgency that is opposed to space — would be infinitely poorer.
It is also from space that humanity saw, for the first time, its entire planet: a small blue and fragile marble, suspended in the dark, with no visible borders.
This image, brought back by the first missions, has permanently changed our view of ourselves and nurtured the emerging ecological awareness.
Paradoxically, moving away from Earth has taught us to love and protect it.
There remains a third dimension, harder to quantify, and yet perhaps the most important.

Seeking to know where we come from, whether there is life elsewhere, what this universe we are part of is: this desire to understand is not a superfluous luxury, it is one of the deepest traits of our humanity.
It is this desire that drove our ancestors to cross oceans, to map continents, to uncover the secrets of the atom and of life.

A humanity that would give up exploration, that would completely retreat into managing its immediate problems, would lose something essential — that part of dream and curiosity without which none of the great advances would have taken place.
Should we then accept everything in the name of space?
No, and the objection retains its share of truth as a safeguard.
The billionaires who indulge in orbital rides, the militarization of space, the race to plant flags for mere glory: all of this is legitimately critiquable.
The question is not 'space, yes or no?', but 'what space, for what purpose, and at what cost?'.
An exploration in service of knowledge and the common good has nothing to do with the space tourism of the very rich.
Space will not solve hunger or poverty, and those who oppose it to urgent earthly issues are right to refuse that it serves as an escape.
But if well designed, it is not the enemy of these causes: it can sometimes be an unexpected ally.
Continuing to look up at the sky, as long as we never forget the Earth beneath our feet, is not an escape.
It is faithful to what we have always been: a species that, to move forward, has always needed a horizon.

sentences: Climate change is everywhere in the news, often amidst passionate debates and complicated figures.
However, the basic mechanism is surprisingly simple, and understanding it helps to move beyond slogans.
Let's try to explain it calmly, without jargon.
It all starts with a natural phenomenon that is, in fact, essential: the greenhouse effect.
Around the Earth, the atmosphere contains certain gases that trap some of the sun's heat, like a blanket.
Without them, the planet would be frozen and life impossible.
So the problem is not the greenhouse effect itself, but its intensity.
For the past two centuries, human activity has been adding enormous quantities of these gases to the atmosphere.
By burning coal, oil, and gas to produce energy, we release carbon dioxide emissions.
The blanket thickens, trapping more heat, and the average temperature of the planet rises.
This is what we call global warming.
An increase of one or two degrees may seem tiny; after all, the temperature changes much more than that between morning and afternoon.
But here we are talking about a global average, and at this scale, a few degrees are enough to upset everything: melting ice, rising sea levels, droughts, and more violent storms.
The climate is not just becoming 'warmer'; it is becoming more unstable.
Regarding the causes, the scientific community is now almost unanimous: this rapid warming is indeed of human origin.
The serious debate is no longer about 'if', but about 'how much' and what we decide to do.
Understanding this alone doesn't solve anything, and it can even be overwhelming given the scale of the problem.
But it is a necessary starting point.
We cannot act intelligently in the face of a threat we do not understand.
And the good news is that the same activities that caused the problem can, if transformed, be part of the solution.

sentences: In France, there is a special meal for children: snack time.
It's at four o'clock, after school.
Lunch is at noon and dinner is at eight o'clock.
That's a long time!
So, at four o'clock, the children are hungry.
My daughter Camille comes home from school at a quarter past four.
She puts down her bag.
She always says the same thing: 'Mom, I'm hungry!'
Snack time is not a big meal.
It's something simple.
Today, Camille is eating bread with chocolate.
It's her favorite snack.
She also drinks a glass of milk.
Sometimes, she has yogurt or a fruit.
During snack time, Camille tells me about her day.
She talks about her teacher, her friends, and sports.
After snack time, she does her homework.
Snack time is not just about food.
It's a moment together, every day.

sentences: In the 2000s, night trains almost disappeared from Europe.
In France, most lines were closed between 2000 and 2017.
They were expensive, the equipment was aging, and low-cost airlines offered unbeatable tickets.
In recent years, the trend has reversed.
Several lines have reopened, and others are announced, in France as well as in Austria, Sweden, or Germany.
Why this return?
The most obvious reason is ecological.
A train journey emits significantly less greenhouse gas on average than the same journey by plane.
For distances of six hundred to one thousand five hundred kilometers, the night train becomes a credible alternative.
But there is also a practical argument, often underestimated.
A night train does not take time away from the day: you board in the evening, sleep, and arrive in the morning.
No airport to reach, no check-in two hours beforehand, no hotel night to pay for.
When compared honestly, the actual time difference is smaller than it seems.
The challenges remain numerous.
Rolling stock is expensive, and it takes years to build.
Tracks are used at night for maintenance.
Finally, it is difficult to make these lines profitable without public support.
Comfort, on the other hand, has improved: the new cars offer smaller compartments, sometimes individual, very different from the six-person couchettes of the past.
I took a night train last year.
I slept poorly, I admit.
But I woke up in another region, without having lost a single day.

sentences: Artificial intelligence is very much in the news, with spectacular promises and concerns.
It's useful to look at what it already does, concretely, in an ordinary day.
It is present when a translation app turns a photographed menu into understandable text.
When a navigation service recalculates a route taking traffic into account.
When a phone finds all the photos where the same person appears.
When a messaging service filters out unwanted emails.
These uses have a common point: the machine recognizes patterns in huge amounts of data.
That's what it does very well.
The more recent tools, capable of writing a text or answering a question, work on a similar principle.
They have learned, from a very large number of texts, which words probably follow which others.
This explains both their fluency and their main flaw.
Because these systems don't 'know' anything in the sense we understand.
They produce the most plausible sequence, which is not the same as the most true.
They can therefore confidently assert false information, invent a reference, or get a date wrong without ever hesitating.
This confidence is precisely the trap: we spontaneously associate a confident tone with reliability.
The reasonable use that emerges is quite simple.
These tools are useful for drafting, rephrasing, translating, summarizing, and suggesting ideas.
They do not replace verification, especially when it comes to facts, figures, or important decisions.
In other words: a quick assistant, never a source.

sentences: One might have thought that open-air markets would disappear with the rise of supermarkets.
Yet they have remained: France has several thousand of them, held weekly or biweekly, in both cities and villages.
Their survival is interesting because, on paper, supermarkets win on almost all criteria: longer hours, wider selection, shelter in case of rain, parking, and often lower prices.
So why continue going to the market?
The first answer is perceived quality, especially for fruits, vegetables, and cheeses.
It is not always objectively superior — a market can sell products from the same supply chains — but the ability to see, smell, and ask matters a lot.
The second answer is the relationship.
At the market, there is someone in front of you.
You can ask how to cook an unfamiliar vegetable, get advice, and be recognized from one week to the next.
This connection does not exist in an aisle.
The third answer is social, and it is probably the most decisive.
The market is one of the few places where people from different generations and backgrounds meet without an appointment.
People also go there to meet others, often without stating it that way.
Municipalities have understood this: many actively support their markets, even when they are not profitable, because they help sustain a town center.
Thus, the market has not survived despite its commercial inefficiency.
It has survived because it serves not just to buy.

sentences: Few topics generate as much discussion among foreigners living in France as the administration.
The word 'paperwork' is among the first they learn.
Part of this reputation is deserved.
The procedures often require providing multiple documents, sometimes several times to the same organization, and the wait times can be long.
But part of it is a misunderstanding, as the logics differ.
The French system is based on written proof.
It requires supporting documents because it operates on the principle that a statement must be documented.
The British system relies more on declaration: you state something, and checks happen later, by sampling.
Neither approach is absurd.
The first is heavier but creates fewer disputes; the second is faster but assumes a trust that can be betrayed.
Another difference: France has long preferred very detailed rules, covering every case, rather than general principles left to interpretation.
This produces precise texts, and a real difficulty when a situation doesn't fit into any category.
It should be added that digitization has greatly improved many procedures.
Declaring taxes online now takes just a few minutes, which was unthinkable twenty years ago.
The advice unanimously given by expatriates is very concrete: keep everything, organize everything, and never throw away a proof of residence.
Tom took three years to understand the system.
He now keeps a binder — a habit he never had in London.
'It still annoys me,' he says.
'But I never have problems anymore.'

sentences: Life expectancy has significantly increased over the course of the twentieth century.
It's one of the most remarkable advances in human history.
But another indicator, less publicized, deserves attention: healthy life expectancy, which means the number of years lived without significant limitations in daily activities.
This indicator is progressing more slowly than total life expectancy.
In other words, we are gaining years, but part of those years are lived with difficulties.
Reducing this gap has become a central objective of public health policies.

What influences this period is quite well identified, and not surprisingly: physical activity, diet, tobacco, alcohol, sleep quality, and — an often forgotten element — maintaining social connections.
Two points deserve to be highlighted.
The first is the importance of maintaining muscle mass.
From a certain age, muscle mass naturally decreases, and this loss is a major factor of dependency: it increases the risk of falling, and a fall is often the tipping point towards loss of autonomy.
Muscle strengthening, even modest, has a proven effect at any age, including after eighty.
The second is that prevention has no age limit.
Quitting smoking at sixty-five still brings measurable benefits.
Starting physical activity at seventy-five improves balance in a few months.
The idea that it would be 'too late' is contradicted by the data.
The body, even when aged, responds to what is asked of it.
You just need to keep asking it for something.

sentences: There is a French peculiarity often noted by foreign observers: the lasting weight of the initial diploma.
In many countries, the professional path gradually corrects the starting point.
What one has done matters more than the school attended at twenty.
In France, the original diploma, and especially the institution where it was obtained, continues to weigh decades later.
This system has its logic.
It is based on the idea of a fair competition, where academic merit opens access to positions.
At certain times, it allowed for real social mobility: children from modest backgrounds accessed high positions through education.
But it also has some negative effects, which are well identified today.
The first is the difficulty of a second start.
Those who have made poor choices, failed, or simply matured late, carry this starting point for a long time.
Returning to studies later remains possible, but the system values these paths less.
The second is a form of assignment.
Academic success at sixteen strongly depends on the background.
A system that freezes early tends to reproduce the inequalities it claims to correct.
The third is a tense relationship with failure, which relates to the culture of grades.
Making the wrong choice is experienced as an almost definitive mistake, whereas elsewhere it is seen as a step.
Things are evolving slowly: continuing education is developing, career changes are becoming common, and the diploma is losing some of its absolute power.
But the idea remains deeply rooted.
In a job interview in France, it is still common to ask what the candidate studied twenty-five years ago.

sentences: Sometimes a work of art can move us: a painting that makes us stop for no reason, a piece of music that tightens our throat, a poem that sticks in our mind.
Often, we would be unable to explain why.
This emotion, seemingly mysterious, interests both artists and researchers.
One initial answer is that art works on deep mechanisms, partly common to all humans.
Certain proportions, certain rhythms, and certain contrasts produce fairly consistent effects.
It's no coincidence that music from very different cultures uses similar structures.
But artistic emotion is not only universal.
It also depends on what we bring to the work: our memories, our culture, our state of mind.
A mundane song can move us because it is linked to a moment in our lives.
The same work does not affect two people in the same way, nor the same person at two different ages.
A common question arises: do we need to 'understand' art to appreciate it?
Do we need to know the history of a painting, the theory of a piece of music?
The honest answer is: no, it is not necessary, but it adds something.
We can be moved without knowing anything.
In fact, that is the most common experience.
But knowing the context, the intentions, and the techniques often opens additional doors — without canceling the initial emotion, contrary to a widespread fear.
Understanding how a sunset works does not prevent us from finding it beautiful.
Understanding a work is the same.
Knowledge does not replace emotion.
It sometimes gives it more space.

sentences: Before buying a product, booking a restaurant, or choosing a hotel, most of us check online reviews.
These stars and comments now guide a huge part of our decisions.
The principle is excellent: sharing the experiences of many customers should provide reliable information, independent of the seller.
In practice, several biases complicate the reading.
The first is the bias of extremes.
People are more likely to leave a review when they are very unhappy or very enthusiastic.
Average experiences, which are the most common, are underrepresented.
The rating therefore poorly reflects the typical experience.
The second is manipulation.
There are fake reviews, positive ones to inflate a product, negative ones to harm a competitor.
Some companies buy them.
Platforms fight against these practices, with varying success.
The third is more subtle: old reviews weigh on the overall rating, even if the product or establishment has changed.
A few reflexes improve reading.
Ignore the overall rating and instead read the recent reviews.
Be wary of an avalanche of very short enthusiastic comments posted in a short time.
Look for detailed critiques that precisely describe a problem: they are more credible than a "bad" or a "perfect."
And remember that a flaw mentioned by one person may be unimportant to us.
The online review remains useful, as long as it is read as an indication, not as proof.
A global figure reassures.
Three specific comments provide more information.

sentences: There is a natural gap in learning any language between two skills: we always understand more than we can produce.
This gap is even evident in our mother tongue.
We understand words that we never use, and registers that we cannot imitate.
Understanding is easier than producing.
Many learners are unaware of this phenomenon and feel discouraged as a result.
They judge themselves as inadequate because they cannot speak fluently, even though they already understand the essentials of a conversation.
They confuse two levels that do not progress at the same pace.
This reality has practical consequences.
First, it values listening and reading, which are often neglected in favor of expression alone.
Listening a lot and reading texts suited to one's level builds a solid foundation of understanding.
This foundation eventually feeds into production: you can only say what you have first encountered elsewhere.
That’s why reading texts slightly above your level, with the help of translations, is one of the most effective methods.
You encounter words in their context multiple times, without the effort of forced memorization.
Next, this reality alleviates guilt.
Not speaking perfectly while understanding well is not a failure: it’s the normal order of things.
However, you should not wait to be 'ready' to speak, because you are never completely ready.
Understanding prepares you, but only usage truly activates speech.
The effective order is therefore clear.
Understand a lot, early.
Speak imperfectly, early as well.
And accept that the two never progress at the same speed.

sentences: France has more than a million active associations, and a significant part of the population is a member or participates in them.
This associative fabric is a pillar of social life, often invisible because it works well.
These associations cover vast areas: local sports, culture, social aid, the environment, advocacy, leisure, and popular education.
They occupy a unique space, between the State and the market.
The State operates according to general rules, equal for all, but sometimes heavy and distant.
The market produces what is profitable.
However, many needs fall outside both: they are too local, too specific, or not profitable enough.
This is where associations come in.

A sports club in a village, a theater workshop, homework help, a neighborhood association: these are activities that no administration would manage as finely, and that no business would find profitable.
This sector relies on a fragile combination: volunteers, a few employees, public subsidies, membership fees, and donations.
This fragility is real.
Volunteering is aging in some associations, which struggle to renew their teams.
Public funding, under budget constraints, sometimes decreases.
Administrative procedures discourage small organizations.
Yet, what this sector produces is hard to replace: connections, commitment, and the ability to respond quickly and close to the ground.
We underestimate what it brings, precisely because it operates quietly.
We would immediately notice its absence if it disappeared.
A large part of what makes local life livable depends on it.

sentences: Many people today are noticing the same thing, a bit worried: they can no longer concentrate like they used to.
Reading a book for an hour, following a long argument, staying absorbed in a single task without giving in to the urge to check one's phone — what used to be taken for granted now seems difficult.
This is not an isolated impression; it is a widely shared experience, and it deserves to be taken seriously.
First, we must dismiss an overly simple explanation, one that would blame a weakening of individuals.
Our brains haven't changed in twenty years.
What has changed is the environment in which they operate.
We now live under an unending stream of distractions: notifications, messages, alerts, content that constantly demands our attention.
However, attention, by its nature, is built over time and continuity, precisely what these interruptions destroy.
Every interruption has a cost that we underestimate.
When our attention is diverted, even for a few seconds, it then takes effort and time to get back on track.
Multiply these breaks by the dozens of times they occur each day, and you get a mind that never really settles, jumping from one thing to another without ever diving in.
This is sometimes called 'continuous partial attention': we are a bit everywhere, and fully nowhere.
The consequences go beyond mere discomfort.
Deep thinking — the kind that allows us to understand a complex idea, to create, to truly reflect — requires sustained concentration.
A culture that would make this concentration rare would, in turn, make deep thinking rarer.
It's not just our comfort that is at stake, but our collective ability to think.
The good news is that concentration can be retrained.
Like a muscle, it strengthens through exercise: setting aside screen-free time, reading long texts again, accepting boredom instead of fleeing from it immediately.
None of this is spectacular, and nothing is immediate.
But the effort is worth it.
Regaining one's ability to concentrate is not just about working better; it's about reclaiming control over one's own mind.

sentences: This is a figure that should make us stop: about a third of the food produced in the world is never eaten.
It is lost or thrown away at some point in its journey, from the farm to the plate.
In a world where millions of people still suffer from hunger, and where food production heavily impacts the environment, such waste is truly scandalous.
We first need to understand where this waste occurs, as the responsibilities are shared.
Some of the losses happen very early, in the fields and during transport: damaged crops, fruits discarded because they are not the right size, goods lost due to lack of preservation methods.
Another part occurs in stores, where items approaching their expiration date or those that do not sell are thrown away.
Finally, the last part happens at home, in our kitchens, where we buy too much, forget, and let things spoil.
What strikes you about this waste is its absurdity.
It does not result from a shortage, but rather from a poorly managed abundance.
We do not throw away food because we lack it, but because we have too much and treat it as something worthless.
Absurd aesthetic standards lead to the rejection of perfectly edible vegetables; a too-strict reading of dates causes good products to be thrown away.
The good news is that none of these causes are insurmountable.
Unlike other environmental issues that require deep transformations, the fight against waste often relies on common sense and organization.

Redistributing unsold goods, revising appearance standards, clarifying dates, better planning purchases: these are all concrete measures, already successfully tested, that require no sacrifice, only attention.
On an individual level, a few simple habits are enough to significantly reduce one's own waste: buying according to real needs, using leftovers, trusting your senses rather than a date.
Nothing heroic, just a basic respect for what food represents.
Food waste may be one of the few major problems that could be largely solved without sacrifice, simply by stopping to treat as waste what has required so much land, water, and labor.
In short, we just need to remember the value of what we throw away.
Being reachable everywhere, at any time, was initially presented as an achievement: never cut off from the world, always within reach of those we love, never lost.
This promise has largely been fulfilled.

But it has come with an unforeseen downside: if we can always be reached, we are also always reachable, and this constant availability, initially experienced as freedom, gradually reveals itself to be a form of servitude.
The shift occurred imperceptibly.
What was once possible has become expected, then mandatory.
Not responding quickly to a message is now seen as negligence, even rudeness.
We feel compelled to stay connected, to check, to react, as if the whole world demands our presence at all times.
The technology that was supposed to liberate us has chained us to an unending expectation.
What we lose in this perpetual availability is something precious: the right to be unreachable at times.
The right to step away from the flow, to withdraw, to be there for no one other than those who are truly around us.
This right, which our ancestors exercised without even thinking about it — because no one could reach them — has become a rare commodity that we must now consciously defend.
It's not about demonizing tools that provide immense services, nor about dreaming of an impossible return to a disconnected world.
It's about restoring a balance, distinguishing between what is a real necessity and what is merely a habit or social pressure.
Almost nothing, in truth, requires immediate attention; the constant urgency is most often an illusion we maintain ourselves.
Regaining the right to disconnect requires concrete decisions: screen-free periods, moments when we turn off, rules we set for ourselves and uphold in front of others.
This takes a certain courage, as we must accept disappointing expectations that have become excessive.
But it is at this price that we regain control of our time, instead of being its servant.
Being reachable is a convenience; being able not to be is a freedom.
In a world that confuses the two, preserving the latter has become an ordinary yet essential act of resistance.

sentences: Never before in history have humans traveled as much.
What was once the privilege of a few has become a mass practice: we travel far, often, and for little money.
This democratization of travel is, in many ways, a blessing.
And yet, a troubling question arises: by traveling so much, are we really traveling in the full sense of the word?
For a long time, traveling was something other than just moving from one place to another.
It was about exposing oneself to the unknown, allowing oneself to be transformed by encountering another place, and returning a little different from the person who left.
Travel implied a certain slowness, an element of the unexpected, and an effort to understand.
It took time to reach a place, time to inhabit it, and time to be changed by it.
It is from this experience that the enrichment we expect from travel was born.
Mass tourism has, in part, dissolved this experience.
We now rush through places, ticking off sites like we’re filling out a checklist, bringing back images more than lived memories.
The destinations themselves, shaped for this quick consumption, offer the same amenities everywhere, so much so that one can travel around the world without ever leaving a familiar setting.
We see a lot; we meet few.
Even more disturbing is that our way of traveling transforms, and often degrades, what we come to seek.
The most popular places empty of their inhabitants, turn into backdrops for visitors, and lose the very authenticity that made them appealing.
The traveler unwittingly destroys the object of their desire: by being seen so much, some places cease to be what we came to see.
Should we then give up travel, or reserve it once again for a few privileged people?
That would be an unfair and sad conclusion.
The problem is not traveling, but the way we do it.
We can travel differently: perhaps not as far, but for longer; not as quickly, but more attentively; seeking not to consume places, but to understand them and allow ourselves to be surprised.
Truly traveling is not a matter of distance or the number of countries visited.
It is a matter of inner disposition: the one that accepts being disoriented, slowed down, and changed.
By this measure, one can travel around the world without ever really traveling, and travel deeply just a few hours from home.
Ultimately, it all depends not on where we go, but on how we look at it.

sentences: Societies, like individuals, have a memory.
They remember certain events, commemorate others, erect monuments, celebrate dates, and pass down stories.

But this collective memory, far from being a simple reflection of the past, results from choices: some things are retained, others are forgotten, certain episodes are highlighted while others are silenced.
What a people's memory retains is therefore nothing neutral; it is a stake, and often a battleground.
For a nation's past is never simple, nor solely glorious.
It contains dark pages as well as proud ones: conquests and defeats, greatness and crimes.
However, a society cannot keep everything present with the same intensity.
It selects, prioritizes, highlights certain memories, and leaves others in the shadows.
This selection reflects what it wants to be, the image it has of itself, and sometimes what it prefers not to see.
This selective memory plays out in each generation.
What was celebrated yesterday can be questioned today; figures once honored are contested, events long silenced resurface and demand recognition.

The debates over statues, commemorations, and street names, which stir so many countries, are not trivial disputes: they concern what a society chooses to celebrate or condemn, thus what it is and wants to become.
The battle is fought over the past, but the stake is the present.
These memory conflicts are often painful, and it would be tempting to want to soothe them by decreeing a convenient forgetfulness: 'let's not stir up the past.'
But this forgetfulness comes at a price.

Silencing the crimes of the past, refusing to acknowledge the inflicted suffering, deprives the victims and their descendants of the recognition they need, and allows wounds to fester for lack of being named.
A memory that only retains the glorious does not soothe; it represses, and what is repressed eventually resurfaces.
Conversely, a memory obsessed only with faults, unable to also recognize what was great, would fall into sterile self-criticism.
The issue is not to choose between pride and shame, but to hold together the whole truth: greatness and crimes, without complacency or denial.
An adult memory is one that can face its past in all its complexity.
The way a people remembers says a lot about its maturity.
Taking responsibility for its past, including its dark areas, without indulging in it or denying it, is a sign of a confident society.
For one does not build oneself on a lie, however flattering, but on the truth, however difficult.

sentences: An age-old dispute opposes two views of language.
For some, a language must be protected, fixed by rules, defended against mistakes and borrowings that distort it; there would exist a correct form that must be preserved from corruption.

For others, a language is a living organism that belongs to those who speak it and has the right to evolve, transform, and incorporate new words; wanting to freeze it would be futile and even harmful.
This disagreement, which resurfaces with every change in the language, deserves to be examined dispassionately.
The defenders of the norm are not entirely wrong.
A language needs common rules to fulfill its primary function: to allow its speakers to understand each other.
If everyone wrote and spoke as they pleased, without a shared convention, communication would become difficult.
Grammar, spelling, and a stable vocabulary are common goods that facilitate exchange and provide access to a written heritage.
In this regard, ensuring a certain level of correctness is not pedantry, but a service to everyone.
But the proponents of evolution also have strong arguments.
Every living language changes, and this is the very sign of its vitality: only dead languages no longer move.
The language that today's guardians of the norm defend is itself the product of centuries of transformations, borrowings, and innovations that could have been denounced as mistakes in every era.
Wanting to stop this movement ignores the fact that the 'pure' language that is claimed to be defended has never existed, and what is called a mistake today may become the correct usage of tomorrow.
There is more.
A language does not belong to an academy or a few guardians, but to the multitude of those who speak it and bring it to life every day.
It is they who, through their usage, ultimately decide what is said and what is lost.
The rules follow usage more than they precede it: they record, with delay, what speakers have already adopted.
Claiming to impose a language from above against the actual usage of its speakers is to misunderstand the very nature of language.
The truth is undoubtedly that these two forces are both necessary, and that their very tension is fruitful.
The norm retains, stabilizes, transmits; usage innovates, adapts, renews.
A language left solely to the norm would freeze and distance itself from its speakers; a language left solely to usage, without any common reference point, would risk fragmenting.
It is from the balance between these two tendencies that a language both stable and alive is born.
Thus, the language does indeed belong to those who speak it, but those who speak it also have an interest in preserving its coherence.

Between the conservatism that would want to freeze everything and the laissez-faire that would abandon all rules, wisdom consists of accompanying evolution without rushing it or rejecting it — treating the language not as a monument to be kept intact, nor as a formless material, but as a living heritage that is transmitted while allowing it to change, cautiously.

sentences: Human influence now extends over almost the entire planet.
There are very few spaces left that we haven't transformed, exploited, or developed.
In light of this observation, a question arises: should we deliberately allow wild places to exist, free from our control and use, or should we put the entire Earth at the service of our needs?
The answer involves the idea we have of our place in the world.
A purely utilitarian view would argue that there is no reason to preserve useless spaces.
If land can nourish, produce, or provide shelter, why leave it fallow?
In this view, the wild is merely untapped potential, a waste to be corrected.
This logic, long dominant, has guided the systematic conquest of the planet, based on the idea that every undeveloped space was just waiting to be utilized.
It rests on a presupposition: that the value of a place is measured by its utility to us.
But another, deeper conception advocates for the preservation of the wild.
It first presents practical reasons: preserved natural spaces provide essential services — climate regulation, preservation of biodiversity, reserves whose full importance we have yet to grasp.
Destroying the wild undermines the very foundations of our existence, often without us realizing it.
Prudence alone demands that we preserve substantial portions of it.
But the most interesting argument is of another kind.
There is a value, it is said, in what escapes our control, in what exists independently of us and our uses.
A world entirely mastered, shaped from top to bottom by human hands, would have something stifling and impoverished about it.
The wild reminds us that there is something other than us, that we are not the only masters, and that the world is not reduced to our projects.
Knowing that there are still free places, even if we never go there, has a value that is not utilitarian.
This value of the wild connects to something of our own balance.
In the face of a fully humanized world, where everything would bear our mark, we would lose an essential point of reference: the measure of what transcends us.
The wild is a lesson in humility, a reminder of our limits, a presence of the other that prevents us from believing we are alone in the world.
Preserving it is not just about protecting ecosystems; it is about preserving a certain idea of our place, neither all-powerful nor central.
Should we then leave a place for the wild?
Yes, for reasons ranging from simple prudence to a higher demand.
Not that humanity should renounce transforming the world — it cannot and should not — but that it should know how to impose limits on itself, reserving spaces for what is not itself.
A civilization may also be judged by what it knows not to appropriate, by its ability to allow, somewhere, the world to be without it.

sentences: We often talk about automation as a natural force, a fate that imposes itself on us: machines 'will' do this, 'will' eliminate that, as if it were an inevitable phenomenon, comparable to the tide.
This way of speaking, so common, carries a dangerous illusion.
For machines do not decide anything by themselves; behind each one, there are human choices — about what we build, for what purposes, for whose benefit.
Becoming aware of these choices means refusing to accept as fate what is, in reality, a matter of decisions.
Let’s consider what is presented as the inevitable course of technology.

Whether a particular task is automated rather than another, whether the gains are used to eliminate jobs rather than to lighten everyone’s work, whether machines are designed to replace humans or to assist them: none of this is dictated by technology itself.
These are orientations taken by companies, investors, and public authorities, based on interests and priorities.
The same technical power can be put to very different ends.
This truth is crucial, as it changes everything.
If automation were a fate, we would have no choice but to resign ourselves to it or adapt.
But if it results from choices, then these choices can be discussed, contested, and directed differently.

We can decide to develop machines that assist workers rather than replace them; we can decide to share productivity gains rather than concentrate them; we can decide to protect those displaced by change.
These decisions are not predetermined; they depend on collective will.
So why is automation so often presented as inevitable?
Partly because it suits those who profit from it.
Presenting a choice as a fate removes it from debate, discourages any contestation, and makes what serves particular interests seem natural.
"There's nothing we can do, it's progress": this seemingly neutral phrase disarms those who might want a different use of technology.
The illusion of technical fate is also a way of confiscating decisions.
Resisting this illusion does not mean opposing technical progress or dreaming of stopping machines.
It means reaffirming that technology is a means to ends we must choose, and not an end that imposes itself on us.
It means asking, at every step, the questions that the illusion of fate silences: what machines do we want, for what purpose, for whose benefit, with what consequences for those they affect?
Who decides what machines do?
The answer should not be: nobody, or technology itself.
It should be: we, collectively, through assumed and debated choices.
Reclaiming these choices means refusing to be passive spectators of a future that is presented to us as already written.

sentences: Almost everyone experiences it: time seems to speed up as we get older.
The summers of childhood felt endless; the years of adulthood fly by at a bewildering speed.
This feeling, so widespread, is somewhat unsettling, because time, objectively, always passes at the same pace.
So why do we perceive it so differently as we age?
The answer reveals a lot about our relationship with time and how we might experience it differently.
A first explanation has to do with proportion.
For a five-year-old child, a year represents one-fifth of their entire existence; for a fifty-year-old man, it is only one-fiftieth.
Each passing year thus weighs less and less, relative to the total of years already lived.
Time does not speed up; it is our scale that changes, with each new duration measured against an increasingly long past.
What seemed vast in childhood becomes a detail in a long life.
A second, deeper explanation relates to novelty.
In childhood and youth, everything is new: each experience is a first time, rich, significant, etched in memory.
Time filled with new experiences seems long because memory has much to retain.
As we get older, however, the days resemble each other, made up of habits and repetitions; they leave few traces, and time seems to fly because memory does not latch onto anything.
It is not time that accelerates, but our life that, by becoming routine, stops filling it with memorable events.
This second explanation is rich in lessons, as it suggests a way to act.
If time seems to fly because our days are similar, then filling it with novelty can, in a sense, slow it down.
Periods rich in new experiences — a trip, a learning opportunity, a life change — seem long in retrospect, dense, full.
Breaking the routine, exposing oneself to the new, stepping out of habits not only allows for a more intense life but also, in a way, stretches time, giving it back the density it had in childhood.
This reflection touches on something essential in our relationship with time.
We often measure time in quantity — hours, years — but what matters may be its density, the way it is filled.
A long but empty life may seem to have passed in an instant; a shorter but denser life may seem to have contained worlds.
The time we truly live is not that of the clock, but that which we experience, and this experience depends on what we make of it.
Time that flies is therefore not just a fate linked to age; it is also, in part, a reflection of how we live.
Letting it flow in repetition makes it seem to accelerate and empty; filling it with novelty, attention, presence gives it back thickness.
We cannot slow down the clock, but we can perhaps change the way we inhabit the time it measures.

sentences: How do we get someone to change their mind, adopt an opinion, or act in a certain way?

Since ancient times, two main paths have been distinguished: to convince, by appealing to reason through arguments; and to persuade, by appealing to emotions, desires, and what precedes or exceeds reason within us.
This ancient distinction remains enlightening, as it touches on a moral question: do all ways of influencing minds have equal value?
To convince through reason means presenting arguments, evidence, and reasoning, and allowing the interlocutor to judge for themselves.
The person who has been convinced agrees because they have understood, because the reasons seemed good to them; their agreement is free, informed, and they could defend it themselves.
This path respects the person as a reasonable being, capable of judgment.
It is demanding, often slow, and uncertain, as reason can resist; but it has its own dignity: it treats the other as an equal, not as an object to be manipulated.
Persuading through emotion is quite different.
It involves acting not on judgment, but on what influences it without their knowledge: fear, desire, self-esteem, belonging to a group.
We do not seek to make them understand, but to make them feel; we do not provide reasons to think, but motives to want.
This path is often more effective than the first, as emotions move more surely than arguments.
But it raises a problem: the one who has been persuaded without being convinced agrees without understanding, driven by mechanisms they do not control.
There lies the moral knot.
For acting on someone's emotions to make them adopt an opinion or take an action, bypassing their judgment, is to treat them as an object to be manipulated rather than as a mind to enlighten.
The boundary here is between legitimate persuasion and manipulation: to manipulate is to gain agreement by circumventing reason, exploiting weaknesses, and deceiving.
The manipulator does not seek for the other to judge well, but for them to do what is expected of them, regardless of how.
Should we then condemn all appeals to emotion, and admit only cold argumentation?
That would be naive and even impoverishing.
Emotions are not the enemy of truth; a just cause can legitimately move us, and emotion can lead to reasons we might not have heard.
The great speaker who defends a just cause by touching hearts does not manipulate; they mobilize.
What distinguishes legitimate persuasion from manipulation is not the appeal to emotion, but the respect or contempt for the other’s judgment: do we move them to enlighten, or to blind?
Understanding this distinction is essential, as we are constantly the object of attempts at persuasion, many of which fall under manipulation.
Advertising, propaganda, speeches that play on our fears and desires: everywhere, there are efforts to act on us by bypassing our judgment.
Knowing how to recognize when we are being addressed through reason and when there is an attempt to short-circuit it gives us the means to resist the latter while remaining open to the former.
To convince honors; to manipulate debases — and distinguishing one from the other is a vital skill for a free mind.

sentences: If there is one thing that human beings seem to need as much as happiness, it is meaning.
We can endure immense suffering if it has meaning, and feel overwhelmed by a comfortable life that seems empty.
Meaning is not pleasure, nor even happiness; it is the feeling that our life matters, that it has direction, value, and a reason for being.
And this need for meaning, often overlooked, may be even more fundamental than the pursuit of happiness.
We measure the importance of meaning by what happens when it is lacking.
A life devoid of meaning, even if it has everything else — comfort, pleasures, security — falls into a form of emptiness, weariness, and dull despair.

In contrast, those who have found meaning in their existence — in a cause, a faith, a work, a dedication — endure trials that would overwhelm others, drawing strength from that meaning that keeps them standing.
A thinker who had gone through the worst horrors observed this: those who survived were often those who had a reason to live, something or someone to hold on to.
Where does meaning come from?
It cannot be decreed, bought, or found ready-made.
It most often arises from a connection: the feeling of belonging to something greater than ourselves, serving a cause, being useful to others, contributing to something larger than oneself.
What gives meaning is often what takes us out of ourselves: love, commitment, creation, transmission, service.
A life entirely focused on its own interest, on its own satisfaction, rarely finds meaning; it is found in transcendence, in giving, in connection to something beyond oneself.
Meaning also arises from the coherence between what we do and what we believe.
A life has meaning when our actions align with our values, when we live according to what we hold as important, when there is no gap between what we believe and what we do.
In contrast, an existence that betrays its own values, that pursues goals it does not truly believe in, becomes devoid of meaning even if it succeeds by external standards.
Meaning relies on this integrity, on this fidelity to what we believe we should be and do.
It should be noted that meaning does not depend on circumstances as much as we think.
One can find meaning in a modest, difficult life devoid of brilliant success; and lack meaning in a life filled with achievements.
For meaning is not measured by what we have, but by how we inhabit our lives, the connections we weave, and what we dedicate ourselves to.

This is good news: meaning is not reserved for a few privileged individuals; it is, in principle, within reach of everyone, regardless of circumstances, as long as one seeks something to dedicate oneself to.
Giving meaning to one's life is therefore not a philosophical luxury, but a vital necessity, as essential as bread.
In a world that offers pleasures and distractions in abundance but struggles to provide meaning, this quest may be the most urgent of all.
Not waiting for life to have ready-made meaning, but constructing it: through what we attach ourselves to, what we dedicate ourselves to, and what we choose to serve.
For a life that has meaning can endure almost anything, while a life that lacks it cannot bear, in the end, anything at all.

alignments.french: Ce qui donne du sens, c'est souvent ce qui nous fait sortir de nous-mêmes : l'amour, l'engagement, la création, la transmission, le service.
alignments.english: What gives meaning is often what takes us out of ourselves: love, commitment, creation, transmission, service.

alignments.french: Une vie tout entière repliée sur son propre intérêt, sur son seul contentement, trouve rarement le sens ; celui-ci se rencontre dans le dépassement, dans le don, dans le lien à autre chose que soi.
alignments.english: A life entirely focused on its own interest, on its own satisfaction, rarely finds meaning; it is found in transcendence, in giving, in connection to something beyond oneself.

alignments.french: Le sens naît aussi de la cohérence entre ce qu'on fait et ce qu'on croit.
alignments.english: Meaning also arises from the coherence between what we do and what we believe.

alignments.french: Une vie a du sens quand nos actes sont en accord avec nos valeurs, quand nous vivons selon ce que nous tenons pour important, quand il n'y a pas de fossé entre ce que nous croyons et ce que nous faisons.
alignments.english: A life has meaning when our actions align with our values, when we live according to what we hold as important, when there is no gap between what we believe and what we do.

alignments.french: À l'inverse, une existence qui trahit ses propres valeurs, qui poursuit des buts auxquels on ne croit pas vraiment, se vide de sens même si elle réussit selon les critères extérieurs.
alignments.english: In contrast, an existence that betrays its own values, that pursues goals it does not truly believe in, becomes devoid of meaning even if it succeeds by external standards.

alignments.french: Le sens tient à cette intégrité, à cette fidélité à ce qu'on croit devoir être et faire.
alignments.english: Meaning relies on this integrity, on this fidelity to what we believe we should be and do.

alignments.french: Il faut noter que le sens ne dépend pas des circonstances autant qu'on le croit.
alignments.english: It should be noted that meaning does not depend on circumstances as much as we think.

alignments.french: On peut trouver du sens dans une vie modeste, difficile, dépourvue de réussite éclatante ; et manquer de sens dans une vie comblée de succès.
alignments.english: One can find meaning in a modest, difficult life devoid of brilliant success; and lack meaning in a life filled with achievements.

alignments.french: Car le sens ne se mesure pas à ce qu'on a, mais à la manière dont on habite sa vie, aux liens qu'on tisse, à ce à quoi l'on se dévoue.
alignments.english: For meaning is not measured by what we have, but by how we inhabit our lives, the connections we weave, and what we dedicate ourselves to.

alignments.french: C'est une bonne nouvelle : le sens n'est pas réservé à quelques privilégiés ; il est, en principe, à la portée de chacun, quelles que soient les circonstances, pour peu qu'on cherche ce à quoi se donner.
alignments.english: This is good news: meaning is not reserved for a few privileged individuals; it is, in principle, within reach of everyone, regardless of circumstances, as long as one seeks something to dedicate oneself to.

alignments.french: Donner un sens à sa vie n'est donc pas un luxe philosophique, mais une nécessité vitale, aussi essentielle que le pain.
alignments.english: Giving meaning to one's life is therefore not a philosophical luxury, but a vital necessity, as essential as bread.

alignments.french: Dans un monde qui offre plaisirs et distractions en abondance mais peine à proposer du sens, cette quête est peut-être la plus urgente de toutes.
alignments.english: In a world that offers pleasures and distractions in abundance but struggles to provide meaning, this quest may be the most urgent of all.

alignments.french: Non pas attendre que la vie ait un sens tout fait, mais le construire : par ce à quoi l'on s'attache, ce à quoi l'on se dévoue, ce que l'on choisit de servir.
alignments.english: Not waiting for life to have ready-made meaning, but constructing it: through what we attach ourselves to, what we dedicate ourselves to, and what we choose to serve.

alignments.french: Car une vie qui a du sens peut supporter presque tout, quand une vie qui n'en a pas ne supporte, à la fin, plus rien.
alignments.english: For a life that has meaning can endure almost anything, while a life that lacks it cannot bear, in the end, anything at all.

sentences: Our public life is living in the era of permanent scandal.
Hardly has one controversy died down before another takes its place; each day brings its new outrage, its designated culprit, its issue to comment on.
We have become so accustomed to this regime of continuous agitation that we no longer perceive it as abnormal.
Yet it deserves to be questioned, as it produces a paradoxical effect: by turning everything into a scandal, we exhaust our very capacity to be alarmed by what truly deserves it.
The mechanism of permanent scandal follows a logic that must be understood.
In a saturated space where countless voices compete for scarce attention, scandal is what captures the gaze.
To exist, therefore, one must produce scandal, constantly create new ones, amplify their scale, and dramatize the stakes.
What would have seemed a minor incident yesterday is today a state affair; what warranted caution becomes a subject of general outrage.
The inflation of scandal is not a sign of a morally more demanding society, but of an attention economy that needs, to function, a constantly renewed emotional fuel.
This inflation has the same effect as any inflation: it devalues the currency it multiplies.
When everything is presented as scandalous, the word loses its meaning and its power.
Collective emotion, constantly solicited, becomes dulled; indignation, too often demanded, grows weary.

As a result, there is an habituation that is the opposite of vigilance: by being alarmed about everything, we end up no longer being alarmed by anything, or we reserve our indignation for what affects our side.
Permanent scandal does not make consciences more sensitive; it anesthetizes them.
This wear and tear has a serious consequence, often unnoticed.
In the clamor of interchangeable scandals, real injustices, those that would require sustained mobilization, are drowned out, treated on the same level as trivial matters blown out of proportion.
Lacking hierarchy, the serious and the trivial become confused, and indignation, dispersed over everything, no longer concentrates on anything.

Thus, permanent scandal, far from serving justice, undermines it: it consumes the moral energy of a society by squandering it on a thousand objects, instead of reserving it for causes that would justify it.
It should also be noted that this regime favors a particular form of injustice: the summary trial.
Scandal demands an immediate culprit, a swift condemnation, without the time for examination or the precautions of judgment.

Carried away by its own dynamics, collective indignation designates, condemns, and punishes before having investigated, even at the cost of ruining reputations based on accusations that no one has verified.
The speed of scandal is incompatible with the slowness of justice, and this incompatibility creates victims that the forgetfulness of the next scandal will never exonerate.
Resisting permanent scandal requires a difficult collective discipline: relearning to distinguish, to prioritize, to reserve alarm for what deserves it, and to give judgment the time it requires.
It also requires a distrust of our own appetite for scandal, of the troubling pleasure that comes from being outraged, from condemning, from participating in the hunt.
A society that knows how to be indignant less often, but more effectively, would be fairer than a society that is outraged by everything.
For the value of indignation does not lie in its frequency, but in its accuracy — and an emotion that is lavished on everything ultimately ends up being unable to defend anything.

sentences: There is a persistent misunderstanding about doubt and uncertainty in science, which fuels a significant amount of contemporary distrust towards it.
Many confuse uncertainty with ignorance and conclude that if scientists are "not sure," it means they don't know, and that their word is therefore no better than anyone else's.
This reasoning is based on a profound misconception.
For acknowledging uncertainty is not admitting ignorance; on the contrary, it is a sophisticated form of knowledge, one that understands the limits of what it asserts.
First, we must distinguish two meanings of the word "uncertainty."
There is the uncertainty of someone who knows nothing, who has no idea, who is completely in the dark: that is ignorance.

And there is the uncertainty of someone who knows a lot but precisely understands the extent of what they do not know, who can say not only what they consider established, but also with what degree of confidence, and where the gray areas begin.
This second uncertainty is not the opposite of knowledge; it is an advanced component of it.
The scholar who says, "we know this with great confidence, that with less, and we still do not know this" knows infinitely more than someone who asserts everything with equal assurance.
This measured uncertainty is even characteristic of a rigorous scientific approach.
Science does not operate on absolute certainties, but on degrees of confidence, constantly adjusted as evidence accumulates.
A scientific assertion is always accompanied, implicitly or explicitly, by an evaluation of its solidity: is it solidly established, probable, hypothetical?
This gradation is not a weakness; it is honesty and precision.
Where ideology or belief assert everything with the same confidence, science distinguishes what it knows from what it assumes, and this distinction is a superiority, not a flaw.
That is why it is misleading, and often dishonest, to exploit scientific uncertainty to disqualify what science establishes.

"Scientists do not agree," "it's just a theory," "nothing is certain": these phrases play on the confusion between the uncertainty that accompanies all rigorous knowledge and the absence of knowledge.
The fact that a theory has areas of uncertainty does not mean it is based on nothing; that a disagreement exists on fine points does not mean that the essentials are in debate.
Using the existence of a margin of uncertainty to reject a solidly established knowledge is to cynically exploit the very integrity of science against itself.

This strategy has been deliberately employed, history shows, by those who had an interest in delaying action: fostering doubt, exaggerating uncertainty, presenting a solid consensus as an open controversy, in order to paralyze under the pretext that we "might not be sure."

This manufacturing of doubt precisely exploits our misunderstanding of scientific uncertainty: by presenting it as ignorance, it turns the virtue of science — its honesty about its limits — into an argument against it.
There is no more effective defense of inaction than to demand an absolute certainty that no science can ever provide.
Understanding that doubt is not ignorance is therefore a way to guard against this manipulation.

It is to recognize that knowledge which knows its limits is better than blind certainty, that measured uncertainty is a form of rigor, and that demanding total certainty before acting is often a disguised way of refusing to act.
Science does not offer us absolute certainties, because it is honest; but it offers us the best available knowledge, along with an indication of its reliability.

Turning away from it on the grounds that it is not absolutely certain is to prefer the illusion of certainty over the reality of knowledge — and to condemn oneself, in the name of a misunderstood doubt, to being unable to believe or decide anything.

sentences: Technological progress often manifests itself as convenience: everything becomes easier, faster, and less burdensome.
What used to require effort, time, and hardship can now be done effortlessly, in an instant, without difficulty.
This promise of convenience is so obviously desirable that we hardly think to question it: who would want difficulty when ease is available?
And yet, we must dare to ask whether convenience, this seemingly flawless good, has a hidden cost, and whether everything that spares us effort truly serves us.
Let's start by acknowledging what is legitimate about convenience.
Many of the efforts that technology spares us were pure burdens, without value, and being freed from them is an undeniable progress.
No one sincerely regrets washing their clothes by hand, traveling miles for information, or painstakingly copying texts.
These hardships had no virtue; freeing ourselves from them has opened up time and energy for better things.
In these cases, convenience is a pure blessing, and denying it would be an absurd form of dolorism that confuses effort with value.
But not all efforts are mere burdens, and this is where convenience becomes ambiguous.
For some efforts have value, not despite their difficulty, but because of it.

The effort to learn builds skills; the effort to search leads to encounters with what we weren't looking for; the effort to do things ourselves provides a competence and satisfaction that the result obtained without effort does not.
When convenience spares us those efforts, it does not just serve us: it also deprives us of what effort produced.
We gain time, but we lose what the time spent brought us.
There is something more subtle.
Widespread convenience gradually makes us incapable of effort by atrophying the skills it spares us from exercising.
By getting everything effortlessly, we lose the habit and taste for effort, until the slightest obstacle seems unbearable.
Ease creates a need for ease, an increasing intolerance for anything that resists, and impatience for anything that does not come immediately.

Thus, convenience, by sparing us effort, makes us unfit for effort, and this unfitness has a cost, because many precious things — mastery, depth, perseverance — require precisely what convenience teaches us to unlearn.
That's not all.
Convenience also has a price that we do not see because it is paid elsewhere.
What is made so easy for us often relies on invisible labor, consumed resources, and costs shifted to others or to the future.
Instant delivery, immediate access, and permanent service assume entire chains of efforts and expenses that convenience hides from us.
We enjoy ease without seeing the price, which is very real, but paid out of our sight.
Convenience does not abolish effort and cost; it displaces them, makes them invisible, and shifts the burden onto others.
Recognizing the price of convenience does not mean rejecting it outright, nor advocating a return to difficulty as a virtue.

It means distinguishing between the efforts that are good to be freed from and those that were worth making, and asking ourselves, in front of each new convenience, what it spares us and what it costs us.
Sometimes it means deliberately choosing effort where it has value, preferring to do things ourselves, to search, to learn, rather than delegating everything to convenience.

In a world that elevates ease to the highest value, reserving spaces for chosen effort is not archaic; it is preserving what convenience, by sparing us too much, ultimately takes away: the ability to do, to struggle, to earn what we obtain.

sentences: The ecological crisis raises a new kind of moral question: do we have duties to future generations, to those who have not yet been born?
Our present actions — what we consume, destroy, and bequeath — will profoundly affect the world that those who come after us will inherit.
But these future people do not yet exist; they cannot ask us for anything, protest, or negotiate.
Can we have obligations to beings who do not exist, and if so, what are these obligations based on?
This question, seemingly abstract, governs our relationship with the future.
A first difficulty lies in the fact that future generations cannot claim any rights, since they do not exist.
We have duties, it is said, to those who have rights; but can a being that does not exist have rights?

This objection has logical force, but it clashes with a powerful intuition: it seems clear to us that bequeathing a devastated world to future generations would be a wrongdoing, that we do not have the right to enjoy the present while ruining their future.
This intuition withstands the logical objection and suggests that our duties to the future cannot be reduced to the logic of rights and claims.
So, on what basis can we found these duties?
We can first note that, while future people do not yet exist individually, it is certain that there will be future generations, and their fate depends on us.
We know that they will exist, that they will have needs, and that they will suffer or thrive depending on the world we leave for them.
This certainty may be enough to establish an obligation: not to a specific individual, but to those, whoever they may be, who will inherit our actions.

We are in the position of someone who sets a trap on a path where they know others will pass: it does not matter that they do not know who; they know that someone will suffer from their act, and that is enough to make them responsible.
We can also base these duties on the idea of continuity between generations, a chain of which we are merely one link.
We have received from our predecessors a world, knowledge, institutions, a heritage; we enjoy it without having created it.
This debt to the past calls for a symmetrical duty to the future: to pass on in turn, not to break the chain, not to squander a heritage that we only temporarily hold.
We are not absolute owners of the world, free to enjoy it until it is exhausted; we are its custodians, tasked with passing it on.
This conception, present in many traditions, grounds our duties to the future in our place within a continuity that transcends us.
The real difficulty may not be so much in establishing these duties as in feeling them.

For our obligations to the future encounter a major psychological obstacle: the distant future is abstract to us, future generations are foreign to us, and we spontaneously give much more weight to the present than to a future that will no longer concern us.
We know intellectually that we should care about the future, but we feel it poorly, and this lack of feeling paralyzes action.
The problem is not that we ignore our duties to the future, but that we struggle to feel them with enough strength to act accordingly.
Overcoming this obstacle is one of the great moral challenges of our time.

It is not enough to theoretically establish our duties to future generations; we must learn to feel them, to concretely care about a future we will not see, to expand our moral horizon beyond our own existence.
This requires a form of imagination and generosity: to care for those we will never know, to act for a world we will not enjoy, to plant trees under whose shade we will not sit.
This ability to care for the distant future is not natural; it is an achievement, almost a virtue.
But it is this virtue that may determine the fate of those who will succeed us — and the dignity of what we leave them.

sentences: It is easy to imagine that threats to democracy come from its declared enemies: tyrants, extremists, those who want to overthrow it.

We forget a more subtle, but perhaps equally serious threat: the apathy of citizens, this growing disinterest in public affairs, this abstention, this feeling that politics does not concern us or will not change anything.
For a democracy cannot survive without the participation of its citizens; their withdrawal empties it of its substance, hands it over to others, and allows it to wither away.
Apathy does not attack democracy head-on; it undermines it from within.
We must first understand the causes of this apathy, as it is not a simple laziness that can be blamed on citizens.

It often stems from a feeling of powerlessness: what’s the point of getting involved, voting, mobilizing, if one feels that nothing changes, that decisions are made elsewhere, that our voice carries no weight?

This feeling is not unfounded: the increasing complexity of issues, the distance between citizens and decision-making places, the weight of forces that escape voting, can create the impression that democratic participation is futile.
Apathy is often less about indifference than about discouragement, the result of a feeling of powerlessness.
It also arises from disappointment.
Many citizens have turned away from politics after being let down by it: unfulfilled promises, corruption, the feeling that those in power serve their own interests rather than the common good.
This disappointment breeds a distrust that turns into withdrawal: since we cannot trust them, what’s the point of getting involved?
Apathy is then the consequence of a loss of trust in those in power and institutions, a disengagement out of frustration.
It is not the primary cause of the problem, but its symptom: it reflects a crisis in the relationship between citizens and their democracy.
However, regardless of its causes, apathy has serious consequences for democracy.
First, it deprives democracy of the participation on which it relies: a democracy where citizens no longer engage is nothing more than a shell, an electoral ritual stripped of meaning.
Next, it leaves the field open to those who remain mobilized: organized interests, active minorities, those who have the means to exert influence.
When the majority withdraws, it is not a void that prevails, but the power of those who do not withdraw; the apathy of some empowers others.

Finally, it weakens democracy in the face of its enemies: an disengaged, disillusioned, indifferent people is fertile ground for those who would like to replace it with other regimes, as they will not defend what no longer interests them.
There is a vicious circle here that must be named.

Powerlessness and disappointment lead to apathy; apathy weakens democracy and hands power to special interests; this weakening increases the feeling of powerlessness and disappointment, which in turn feeds apathy.
How can we break this circle?

Not by blaming disengaged citizens, which would only worsen their distrust, but by restoring what has been lost: the feeling that participation matters, that citizens' voices count, that politics can change things.
This requires institutions that return power to citizens, a political life that deserves trust, leaders who serve the common good rather than betray it.
Thus, fighting against apathy is not just a matter of individual civic duty, but of a collective restoration of the meaning of democracy.
Everyone can, of course, refuse to be discouraged, engage nonetheless, exercise their share of citizenship; and this individual commitment has its value.
But apathy will only dissipate sustainably if democracy gives its citizens reasons to believe that their participation matters.
For one only engages if one thinks it can change something, and massive disengagement is primarily a sign that too many citizens have stopped believing this.
Restoring democracy's ability to change things is the only lasting remedy to the apathy that threatens it.
