sentences: We consider metaphor to be an ornament of discourse, a figure of style used in poetry, a deviation from literal language that would express things directly.
This conception, inherited from a long tradition, makes metaphor an accessory, an expressive luxury that one could, if necessary, do without.
However, this may be profoundly false.

For it could be that metaphor, far from being an occasional ornament, structures our thinking entirely, that we think in metaphors without realizing it, and that supposedly literal language is itself filled with forgotten metaphors.
This hypothesis, which contemporary reflection has explored, overturns our relationship with language and thought.
Let’s observe our most ordinary language, the one we believe to be literal.

We say that our arguments are solid or that they collapse, that we grasp an idea or that it escapes us, that time passes, that prices rise, that we are at the peak of our form or at the bottom of despair.

These expressions, which we no longer perceive as figurative because they are so worn out, are nonetheless metaphors: they draw from the realm of the concrete, of space, of physical movement, to express the abstract, thought, and emotions.
We conceive of ideas as objects that can be grasped, arguments as structures that stand or collapse, time as a movement, and states of mind as positions in space.
These metaphors are so deeply embedded in our language that we no longer perceive them as such; they have become the very fabric of our thought.
This observation has considerable implications.
For if we think the abstract through the concrete, emotions through space, and ideas through objects, then our metaphors do not merely express our thoughts: they shape them.
The way we conceive of something depends on the metaphor through which we apprehend it.

Conceiving of discussion as a war — attacking a position, defending a point, winning or losing a debate — is not neutral: this war metaphor shapes our very way of discussing, making us see the interlocutor as an opponent to defeat rather than as a partner in the search for truth.
Changing the metaphor changes the thing: conceiving of discussion as a joint construction, a dance, an exploration, would transform our approach to it.
The metaphors through which we live are not just ways of speaking; they are ways of thinking, and thus of acting.
This discovery sheds light on entire aspects of our existence.
Our fundamental metaphors — about time, life, mind, and society — silently guide our understanding and our behavior.
To conceive of life as a journey, a struggle, a game, or a burden engages different attitudes; to conceive of the mind as a machine, a garden, or a container directs how we treat it.
These metaphors, which we did not choose, which we inherited from our language and culture, govern our thought without our awareness, like invisible presuppositions.
Becoming aware of their power is to gain freedom over them: the freedom to question them, to change them, to choose which metaphors we want to think and live by.
It is not about, in recognizing the omnipresence of metaphor, falling into the idea that everything is metaphor, that there is no literal language, no literal truth.
This excessive conclusion would dissolve the distinction between the true and the figurative, without which thought itself wavers.

There is indeed a more literal language, statements whose metaphorical value is null or negligible; but this literal language is narrower than one might have thought, and the abstract, in particular, is hardly expressed without metaphor.
Recognizing this does not deny all literalness; it measures how much metaphor, far from being an ornament that the abstract could do without, is often the only access to it.
The power of metaphors thus teaches us a lesson in humility and vigilance.

In humility, because we discover that our thought, which we believed to be self-mastering, is permeated with metaphors that guide it without our awareness, inherited from a language and culture that think within us before we think.

In vigilance, because recognizing this power invites us to examine the metaphors through which we live, to unearth those that mislead us, to choose, as much as possible, the figures that illuminate rather than those that obscure.

For we cannot think without metaphors; but we can, by becoming aware of their power, stop being their playthings and become, a little, their masters — and discover that changing the way we express things is already beginning to change the way we live them.

sentences: Our era measures value by success.
Those who succeed, who prevail, who win are considered great; those who fail, who lose, who are defeated are deemed contemptible, or at least negligible.
This identification of value with success is so deeply ingrained that it seems obvious.

And yet, a contrary intuition, ancient and persistent, endures: that there are defeats greater than victories, a greatness of the defeated that is not found in success, and that the value of a life is not measured by its triumph.
This intuition deserves to be explored, as it touches on what gives life its worth.
History and human memory preserve, alongside the victors, the traces of the defeated whose defeat was greater than many victories.

Those who fought for a just cause and lost, who resisted oppression and were crushed, who defended a value until death without triumphing, possess a greatness that their defeat does not erase, and which it sometimes even enhances.

We venerate certain defeated individuals more than many victors, not despite their defeat, but through it; for their defeat testifies to a loyalty to what is worth more than success, a refusal to sacrifice the essential for victory.
There is a greatness that reveals itself precisely in failure, when failure is the price of loyalty.
Let us understand what constitutes this greatness of the defeated.
It lies in the fact that the value of what they fought for does not depend on its success.
A just cause does not become unjust because it is defeated; a loyalty does not lose its worth because it fails; a fight for what is valuable retains its nobility even when lost.

He who subordinates everything to victory, who betrays his values to win, may win, but he loses the essential; he who remains faithful to what is valuable, even at the cost of defeat, may lose, but he saves the essential.

The greatness of the defeated is that of those who preferred to lose while remaining faithful rather than to win by betraying; it testifies that certain things are worth more than success, and that remaining faithful to them, even when defeated, is a victory of a different kind.
This greatness illuminates a truth that the cult of success obscures: the value of a life is not measured by its success.

A life can be a failure in the eyes of the world — without glory, without triumph, without success — and yet be great, if it has been faithful to what is valuable, if it has served a just cause, if it has refused to betray the essential.
Conversely, a life crowned with success can be mediocre, even vile, if that success was purchased at the cost of betraying everything that matters.
Success is not the measure of value; it can coexist with baseness, just as greatness can coexist with failure.
What gives a life its worth is what it has been faithful to, not what it has obtained.
This recognition of the greatness of the defeated has a comforting and liberating significance.

Comforting, because it frees us from the tyranny of success, from the anxiety of achieving, from the shame of failure; it tells us that our worth does not depend on our success, that we can fail and remain dignified, lose and still be great.
Liberating, because it allows us to place our loyalty elsewhere than in victory, to serve what is valuable without subordinating everything to success, to prefer justice to achievement.
He who has understood the greatness of the defeated is free with respect to success; he can seek it, but without sacrificing the essential, without making it the measure of his worth.
In celebrating the greatness of the defeated, it is not about praising failure, nor despising success, nor finding false comfort in one's defeats.
Not all defeats are great; there are failures that testify only to weakness or fault, and the greatness of the defeated belongs only to those whose defeat was the price of loyalty.

But recognizing this greatness means rejecting the identification of value with success, affirming that certain things are worth more than victory, and that remaining faithful to them, even when defeated, is the highest form of success.

In a world that only adores victors, remembering the greatness of the defeated preserves an essential truth: that the worth of a life is not measured by what it gains, but by what it remains faithful to.

sentences: Why does beauty move us?
Why do certain forms, certain sounds, certain spectacles evoke in us this particular emotion, this thrill, this pleasure sometimes mixed with tears, which we call aesthetic emotion?
This question, which seems simple, is actually one of the deepest and most enduring there is.
For none of the explanations given seem to fully exhaust it; there remains, in our emotion in the face of beauty, something that escapes, a mystery that reflection approaches without dispelling.
At the end of this meditation on beauty, it is worth pausing on this enigma, not to solve it, but to measure its depth.
Attempts have been made to explain aesthetic emotion in various ways.
Some have seen it as the recognition of harmony, proportion, or order that would meet a requirement of our mind; we would be moved by what presents formal perfection, a satisfying agreement of parts.

This explanation captures something, but it leaves something out: for not all beauty is harmony and proportion, and some beauties move us through their strangeness, their rupture, their excess, rather than through their order.
Harmony explains part of our emotion, but not its entirety or its mystery.
Others have sought the explanation in our nature, in our evolution, seeing it as an inherited disposition, a mechanism shaped by our history.
We would be moved by certain forms because this emotion would have had a function for our ancestors: to attract us to what is favorable, to divert us from what is harmful.
This approach has its fertility, it sheds light on some of our preferences; but it too leaves a considerable remainder.

For aesthetic emotion far exceeds what a simple adaptive function would explain; it pertains to objects — a work of art, a complex melody, a beautiful thought — that have no relation to our ancestors' survival.
The explanation by nature sheds light on the origin of certain dispositions, but not on the richness and depth of aesthetic emotion.
Others have linked aesthetic emotion to a meaning, to a significance, to what beauty tells or reveals to us.
We would be moved not by the form alone, but by what it expresses, by the truth it reveals, by the meaning it carries.
This approach is profound, and it accounts for the spiritual dimension of aesthetic emotion, for what it has beyond mere sensory pleasure.
But it too encounters a limit: for some beauties move us without us being able to say what they mean, by their mere sensible presence, independently of any formulable meaning.
Emotion often precedes and overflows any significance we might attach to it.
What strikes one in these attempts at explanation is that none exhausts the phenomenon, that all leave something out, that aesthetic emotion always seems to exceed what is said about it.
Perhaps this is the essence: that beauty, and the emotion it evokes, touch on something that resists explanation, that cannot be reduced to a cause, a function, or a meaning.
Aesthetic emotion puts us in the presence of something that transcends us, that exceeds our categories, that retains a part of mystery.

And it could be that this mystery is not a temporary limit of our knowledge, a riddle that one day will be solved, but an essential dimension of the phenomenon: that beauty is precisely what moves us without us being able to fully say why, what exceeds all explanation.

Recognizing this mystery is not giving up on understanding, nor sinking into the irrational; it is acknowledging the limits of explanation in the face of certain phenomena, and respecting what, in our experience, resists reduction.

The emotion in the face of beauty is one of those experiences that remind us that not everything can be explained, that our relationship with the world involves dimensions that exceed knowledge, that we are beings capable of being moved by what we do not fully understand.

And perhaps this is part of the value of beauty: that it opens us to a mystery, that it puts us in the presence of what transcends us, that it reminds us that human existence cannot be reduced to what can be explained and mastered.

Beauty moves us, and the fact that we do not quite know why is not a failure of our understanding, but perhaps a sign that we are touching, in this emotion, something essential that exceeds understanding itself.

sentences: We have distinguished between suffered solitude, which is suffering, and chosen solitude, which is richness.
But there is a third solitude, deeper than the other two, that no choice or company can abolish: essential solitude, which pertains to our very condition as conscious beings.
Each of us is a unique consciousness, a singular perspective on the world, confined in a sense to our own experience, which no one can fully share.

This solitude is neither a misfortune to be cured nor a good to be cultivated; it is a given of our condition that must be faced to understand what we are and what our relationships with others can or cannot be.
What does this essential solitude consist of?
It consists in the fact that each person experiences the world from their own point of view, in their own consciousness, and that this lived experience is, by nature, fundamentally incommunicable.
I cannot feel your pain as you feel it, nor can you feel mine; I cannot see the world through your eyes, nor enter your consciousness.
We can communicate, understand each other, draw closer; but there remains, at the core of each person, a lived experience that no one shares, a unique perspective that remains their own.

I am the only one who is me, the only one who feels what I feel from the inside; and this solitude, no company, no love, no communication can abolish, for it pertains to the very structure of consciousness.
This essential solitude reveals itself with particular acuity in certain experiences.
Suffering, first: the one who suffers is alone with their pain, which no one can feel in their place, however compassionate they may be.
Death, then, the ultimate trial of solitude: one dies alone, no one can die in our place nor accompany us beyond a certain threshold.
But also the most intimate experiences, the deepest thoughts, what is most personal in us, which remains, at its core, incommunicable.
There is in each person a core of solitude that nothing can break, a part of us that remains alone, regardless of our ties and surroundings.
This recognition may seem despairing, as if it condemns us to irredeemable isolation, as if others are forever inaccessible to us.
But that would be a misunderstanding of essential solitude.

For recognizing that there is in each person an incommunicable core does not mean that communication is impossible, that connections are futile, that we are locked in ourselves without access to others.
We communicate, we understand each other, we love each other, despite and through this solitude; simply, this communication does not abolish it entirely, it builds bridges over an abyss that remains.

Recognizing essential solitude does not deny the possibility of connection; it means understanding its true nature, which is not fusion but a meeting between beings who remain, at their core, distinct.
There is even something precious in this essential solitude when we understand it well.
For it is the correlate of our singularity, of our uniqueness, of what makes each person irreplaceable.

If we could completely merge into one another, fully share our experience, abolish all solitude, we would cease to be distinct individuals, unique consciousnesses; essential solitude is the price and the guarantee of our individuality.
It is what makes each person someone, a unique perspective on the world, a being who is not interchangeable.
Essential solitude is not just a limit to our relationships; it is also what underpins the value of each being as singular.
Understanding essential solitude transforms our relationship with others and with ourselves.
With ourselves, by reconciling with this part of irreducible solitude, by ceasing to experience it as a lack to be filled, by recognizing that it is the correlate of our singularity.

With others, by understanding that true connection is not the fusion that would abolish all distance, but the meeting that respects each person's solitude, the bridge thrown over the abyss that remains.
Loving others is not about abolishing their essential solitude or ours, but about recognizing and respecting that solitude while building bridges of love and understanding towards it.

The most beautiful relationship is not one that would deny essential solitude, but one that, recognizing it, unites two solitudes that respect each other — for, as a poet said, the highest love is perhaps that where two solitudes protect, limit, and greet each other.

sentences: Learning a foreign language, as we have seen, is not just about acquiring a tool for communication, a set of words and rules; it is about entering a world, a way of thinking, feeling, and experiencing.

This applies to all languages, but each language opens a particular world; and it is worth asking, at the end of this journey through the French language, what world, what sensitivity, and what way of being does learning French specifically open up.
For learning French is not just about gaining another language; it is about accessing a certain relationship with the world, of which it bears the trace.
Every language, as we have said, has lexicalized certain experiences, developed certain nuances, and favored certain relationships with the world.
French thus bears the mark of a certain sensitivity, a certain genius, shaped by a long history.

It has often been said that French is a language of clarity, precision, and rigor, made for analysis, distinction, and the exact expression of thought; a language that values order, structure, and clarity.

This reputation, like any generalization, must be nuanced; but it captures something of the genius of this language, its vocation for clear and distinct expression, and its appreciation for rigorous thinking.
French also bears the trace of a certain culture, a certain relationship to life, art, and thought.

Learning French means accessing a literature, a philosophy, and a tradition of thought that have marked the history of ideas; it means being able to read in their language works that have shaped our way of thinking; it means entering into a dialogue with a culture that has produced a significant part of what humanity has thought and created.

French is the language of a considerable intellectual and artistic tradition, and learning it gives you access to that tradition, not through the mediation of translation, but in the very language in which it was expressed.

But French is not just the language of France; it is spoken on several continents by diverse peoples who have made it their own, enriched it with their contributions, and turned it into the vehicle of their own cultures.
French is a language of sharing that connects different peoples, carries multiple cultures, and belongs not to a single nation but to all who speak it.
Learning French means accessing not just one world, but a plurality of worlds linked by a common language, a diversity of cultures that express themselves in the same language.
It is to enter a linguistic community that transcends the borders of a nation, uniting diverse peoples in the sharing of a language.

We must be careful, in celebrating the world that French opens up, not to fall into naive glorification, as if this language were superior to others, as if the world it opens were better than those opened by other languages.

Every language opens a world, and none is absolutely better than another; French is not superior, it is different, offering a particular access to a culture, a sensitivity, a tradition among others that are equally valuable.
Celebrating the world that French opens is not to regard it as the best, but to recognize that it opens, like any language, its own world, worthy of being known, which enriches those who access it.

At the end of this journey, someone who has learned French to the point of being able to read these demanding texts has thus gained more than just a language: they have gained a world, access to a culture, a sensitivity, a tradition; they have expanded their own world with a new one.

And this conquest is not just useful, an additional tool; it is an enrichment, an opening, a way to become broader, to multiply one's access to reality, no longer being a prisoner of a single way of seeing.

Learning French, like learning any language, is to give oneself an additional world; and those who possess multiple languages, multiple worlds, inhabit a richer, more diverse universe than those who know only one.

This is perhaps the most beautiful reward of this long learning process: not only being able to say and understand more, but having become, through the acquired language, a broader being, open to a world that, without it, would have remained closed to them.

sentences: Becoming oneself: this task, which seems the most natural, is in reality one of the most difficult there is, and it requires a courage that we underestimate.

For we are shaped by countless pressures — those of our environment, our education, the gaze of others, social expectations, and dominant models — that tend to make us conform, to turn us into what the world expects rather than what we truly are.
Becoming oneself, in this context, is not about following a natural slope; it is about resisting these pressures, conquering an existence that is truly one's own.
And this conquest demands a rare courage, the significance of which is worth measuring.
We have seen that the 'self' is not a given thing, a core that simply needs to be discovered, but something that is constructed.
Thus, becoming oneself is not about unearthing a hidden nature, but about making oneself, choosing oneself, constructing oneself, against what would shape us from the outside.
However, this construction of the self encounters powerful forces of conformity.
The desire to be accepted, to not displease, to belong, pushes us to conform, to embrace expectations, to silence what makes us unique.
The weight of others' gaze, the fear of disapproval, the pressure of the group, tends to make us fall in line, to erase what distinguishes us.
Becoming oneself means resisting these forces, daring to be different, and embracing one's uniqueness against the pressure to conform.
This courage to be oneself takes various forms.
It is the courage to have one's own opinions, to think for oneself, and not to adopt accepted ideas out of mere conformity.
It is the courage to make one's own choices, to follow one's path, and not to let one's existence be dictated by the expectations of others.
It is the courage to embrace one's uniqueness, what distinguishes us, what makes us different from others, instead of hiding it to fit in.
It is sometimes the courage to disappoint, to displease, to stray, when being true to oneself demands it.
All these forms share the commonality of resisting the pressure to conform, daring to be oneself against what would seek to make us conform.
This courage is rare because it is costly.
Conforming is easy, comfortable, and rewarded; one gains approval, belonging, and peace.
Being oneself, on the other hand, exposes one to disapproval, to the solitude of those who stray, and to the reproach of those who would like to see us similar to them.
The courage to be oneself must confront these costs, accept displeasing others, disappointing them, and sometimes finding oneself alone.
That is why so many people give it up, preferring the security of conformity to the discomfort of authenticity, the peace of conformity to the demand of being oneself.
Becoming oneself requires accepting these costs, preferring to be true to oneself rather than to be approved.
However, we must be careful not to misunderstand the courage to be oneself as merely a self-assertion against others, an individualism that would disdain others.
Being oneself is not about standing against others, nor about cultivating a superficial originality, nor about making one's difference a banner.
The true courage to be oneself is not ostentatious; it is often discreet, internal, and is more about quiet fidelity to what one believes and who one is than about spectacular rebellion.
It is not about distinguishing oneself for the sake of distinction, but about being true to oneself, which can very well coexist with respect for others and communal living.

The courage to be oneself is not the loud assertion of an ego against the world; it is the often silent fidelity to what one holds to be true and just, against the pressures that would lead us away from it.
This courage to be oneself is at the heart of wisdom, for there is no wise life that is not first a life that is truly one's own.
One cannot live wisely by living someone else's life, by adopting values that one has not made one's own, by conforming to what is expected of us.
Wisdom requires authenticity, fidelity to oneself, and the construction of an existence that is truly ours.
And this construction, against the pressures that shape us, demands this rare and discreet courage to be oneself, to think for oneself, to make one's own choices, and to embrace one's uniqueness.

Becoming oneself, against everything that would seek to conform us, is perhaps one of the most difficult and essential tasks of existence — and one of the conditions for a successful life that is coherent and true to its values, which we have said is the result of a life that has been shaped.

sentences: Yanis doesn't know how to swim very well.
He takes lessons at the pool.
The class takes place on Tuesday evenings.
Yanis goes there after work.
The teacher's name is Marc.
Marc is patient and kind.
At first, Yanis is afraid of the water.
He doesn't like to put his head underwater.
Marc helps him.
"It's not dangerous," says Marc.
"Breathe well."
Little by little, Yanis is learning.
He is learning to move his arms.
He is learning to move his legs.
After a few weeks, Yanis swims a little better.
He is no longer afraid.
One evening, Marc says: "Today, you are crossing the pool by yourself!"
Yanis is a little nervous.
But he tries.
He swims slowly, from one side to the other.
He can do it!
Yanis is very proud.
"I can swim now!" he says to Julien, his friend.
Julien is happy for him.
Well done, Yanis!
Now, are we swimming together this weekend?

sentences: For my husband's fortieth birthday, I organized a surprise party.
No one was supposed to know anything, especially not him!
I started preparing the party two months in advance.
I secretly contacted his friends and family.
The hardest part was finding a reason for him to be away during the preparations.
I told him that we were going to have dinner at his parents' house.
In the meantime, his friends decorated our garden with lights and balloons.
Three days before the party, my husband started to suspect something.
"You're acting strange right now," he said to me.
I had to lie several times so he wouldn't understand.
It wasn't easy!
On the big day, I took him "to his parents' house."
In reality, everyone was waiting for us at our place.
When we entered, thirty people shouted "Surprise!"
My husband was speechless for a good minute.
Then he laughed and cried at the same time.
"How did you manage to hide all this from me?" he asked me later.
This party will remain one of the best memories of our life together.

sentences: I learned piano as a child, then I stopped for twenty years.
This year, I decided to start again.
My piano teacher, when I was a child, was called Madame Blanc.
I still remember her living room, with the big black piano.
At forty, I found a new, younger teacher.
At first, I was a little ashamed to start over.
My fingers didn't move like before.
The notes that I knew by heart as a child, I had completely forgotten.
"It's normal," my teacher told me.
The muscle memory comes back, but it takes time."
I practiced twenty minutes every evening, after work.
At first, it was frustrating.
After three months, I finally managed to play a whole piece without any mistakes.
I was as proud as a child.
My own children are now watching me play, a little surprised.
"I didn't know you could play, dad!"
The piano has given me back something I had lost a long time ago.

sentences: Last month, I started a new series on a streaming platform.
At first, I thought I would just watch one episode in the evening, before going to sleep.
But each episode ended with a scene that made me want to see the next one immediately.
"Just one more episode, and I'll stop," I would tell myself every night.
It was almost never true.
One weeknight, I watched four episodes in a row, until two in the morning.
The next day, I was exhausted at work.
My colleague asked me if I was okay.
"I just watched a bit too much television last night," I explained to her, a bit embarrassed.
She laughed.
"This series is driving everyone crazy right now, apparently."
After that difficult night, I decided to set a rule for myself: one episode per night, no more.
It's not always easy to stick to, but at least I'm sleeping better now.

sentences: This winter, I decided to learn how to make a wooden piece of furniture, a small coffee table.
I had never done woodworking before.
I watched several videos and bought wood at a hardware store.
I set up a small workshop in my garage, with the necessary tools: a saw, sandpaper, wood glue.
During the first week, I cut the boards according to the planned measurements.
Some cuts were not perfectly straight.
I had to redo two boards, a bit frustrated, but I continued patiently.
After assembling the legs of the table, I noticed that it was not completely stable.
It wobbled slightly.
I spent an entire evening fixing this problem by adjusting each leg.
Finally, I sanded the entire surface to make it smooth, then I applied varnish.
After three weeks of work, my coffee table was finally finished.
It isn't perfect; you can see some small flaws if you look closely.
But it's in my living room now, and I'm very proud of it.

sentences: I ordered a dress online for a wedding, but it didn't fit me at all.
I had chosen my usual size, but the dress was clearly too small, almost impossible to close.
The wedding was in three weeks.
I had to act quickly.
I looked for how to return the dress on the website.
The instructions weren't very clear.
I had to print a return label, put the dress back in its original packaging, and then drop it off at a collection point.
I found a collection point near my home, in a small grocery store.
The refund took ten days to arrive in my account, a bit longer than I expected.
In the meantime, I ordered a size up, in another color, to be more sure.
This second dress arrived four days before the wedding, and it fit me perfectly this time.
I wore this dress with pleasure, but I learned my lesson well: always check sizes carefully before ordering online for an important occasion.

sentences: Last January, I started a very strict diet, recommended by a friend who praised its impressive results.
The principle was simple on paper: to almost completely eliminate carbohydrates, eat mainly proteins and vegetables for at least two weeks.
The first three days went quite well, fueled by still fresh motivation.
Then, from the fourth day on, an unusual fatigue set in, accompanied by regular headaches.
At work, I struggled to concentrate, irritable over trivial things that normally didn't bother me.
On the seventh day, exhausted and frustrated, I gave up the diet, feeling almost guilty about my lack of willpower.

Later, when I spoke with a nutritionist, I learned that this type of very restrictive diet rarely works in the long term, and that a more gradual change generally yields better results, even if they are less spectacular at first.
This experience taught me something important: the miracle solution that is often sold to us in January rarely resembles a true sustainable solution.
Later, while discussing with others who had the same misadventure, I discovered that this feeling of personal failure was strangely widespread.
Many blamed themselves for their lack of willpower, while the problem might have stemmed more from the very design of the diet than from any character flaw.
Today, I try to eat a bit more balanced, without total restrictions, which seems much easier to maintain over time.

sentences: The market for pet products has seen impressive growth in recent years.
Today, there are designer clothes for dogs, health insurance for cats, and even 'animal psychology' services to help the most anxious pets.
This evolution reflects, according to several experts, a change in the role that animals play in our homes.
Once primarily seen as guard animals or simple companions, they are now treated by many owners as true family members.

Some companies have understood this evolution well and now offer increasingly specialized products: customized kibble based on breed, luxury hotel rooms for pets, and birthday cakes specially designed for dogs.
This industry also raises criticisms.
Some observers question the relevance of spending so much money on sometimes unnecessary products, while many shelters still struggle to find sufficient funding.
Others, on the contrary, defend these expenses as legitimate, believing that animal welfare deserves the same care as that given to other family members.
I must admit that I have also given in to some of these unnecessary purchases for my own cat, without being fully convinced of their usefulness.
This contradiction, between my principled clarity and my actual consumer behavior, perhaps illustrates the general difficulty in resisting this market, even when one knows its mechanisms.
This market, which continues to grow, certainly illustrates how much our relationship with pets has profoundly evolved.

sentences: For a long time, I admired those personalities known for sleeping only four or five hours a night, often presented as models of success and discipline.
This idea, very widespread in the professional world, associates reduced sleep with a form of superiority: those who sleep little would work more, achieve more, and be more determined than others.
By taking a closer interest in this subject, I discovered that this belief is based on very fragile scientific foundations.
The vast majority of adults actually need seven to nine hours of sleep to function properly.
The few people who can function well on very little sleep actually possess an extremely rare genetic trait, found in less than one percent of the population.

In other words, most people who claim to sleep four hours and 'get by very well' are probably functioning, without knowing it, with reduced capacities, without even realizing it, as chronic fatigue becomes a new normal for them.
Some colleagues who proudly claimed to sleep little were making mistakes that a bit more rest would likely have spared them.
This contradiction, between the displayed prestige of sacrifice and its real cost on the quality of work, is rarely questioned in these same professional environments.
This discovery changed my view on this myth of success through lack of sleep.
It is not a sign of strength, but often a sign of unrecognized exhaustion, wrongly presented as an admirable quality.

sentences: Clothing has never been a purely aesthetic or practical choice; it often carries an explicit or implicit political dimension that societies have exploited throughout history to assert identities or claims.
Some historical examples clearly illustrate this function.

The trousers, long reserved for men in many Western societies, became a true act of protest against established gender norms when women began to wear them publicly, long before they became completely normalized.

Similarly, certain traditional garments, proudly worn by cultural minorities within societies that sought to assimilate them, have functioned as acts of identity resistance, claiming an affiliation that the majority would have preferred to see disappear.
Even today, this political dimension of clothing remains very much alive, although sometimes in more subtle forms.

The choice to wear, or to refuse to wear, certain religious symbols in public space continues to spark intense legal and social debates in several countries, precisely because clothing is perceived there as carrying a message that goes beyond mere appearance.
However, this political dimension is not always conscious or claimed by the person wearing it.
Many clothing choices, seemingly neutral, nonetheless fit into broader social and cultural logics, without the person making them being fully aware.

Recognizing this political dimension of clothing, far from being anecdotal, may help better understand why some clothing debates, seemingly superficial, actually provoke passions and tensions that are much deeper than their immediate subject might suggest.

sentences: Each generation seems to laugh at things that are noticeably different, to the point that jokes considered hilarious by some sometimes leave others completely indifferent, or even perplexed by what generates such comic enthusiasm.
This generational evolution of humor is not merely a matter of arbitrary taste change, but often reflects deeper transformations in the concerns, values, and anxieties specific to each generation.

The humor of generations that have grown up with constant exposure to social media, for example, is often characterized by an intensive use of layered irony, second, or even third-degree humor, perhaps reflecting a general distrust of any statement taken at face value, in a media environment saturated with contradictory information.

Previous generations, shaped in a more centralized and unified media landscape, often developed humor that relied more on cultural references widely shared by the entire population, a community of references that is now much more fragmented by the diversity of content available online.

These differences do not necessarily mean that one generation has superior humor to another, but rather that each generation develops comedic codes suited to its own historical, technological, and social context, often difficult to fully decode for those who have not shared the same formative context.

Carefully observing what each generation finds funny thus constitutes, for sociologists studying these phenomena, a valuable and often overlooked indicator of the broader cultural transformations that pass through a society at a given moment in its history, revealing through laughter truths that serious discourse sometimes struggles to express directly.

sentences: The garden, longer than it was wide, stretched between two walls of rammed earth covered with espaliered apricot trees, all the way to a hedge of thorns that separated it from the fields.
In the middle, there was a slate sundial on a masonry pedestal; four flowerbeds filled with thin wild roses symmetrically surrounded the more practical square of serious vegetation.
At the very back, under the small fir trees, a plaster priest was reading his breviary.
Emma went up to the bedrooms.
The first one was unfurnished; but the second, which was the marital bedroom, had a mahogany bed in a nook with red drapery.
A shell box decorated the dresser; and on the writing desk, near the window, there was a bouquet of orange blossoms in a carafe, tied with white satin ribbons.
It was a bridal bouquet, the bouquet from the other!
She looked at it.

Charles noticed this, took it, and went to put it in the attic, while Emma, sitting in an armchair (her belongings were arranged around her), thought about her wedding bouquet, which was packed in a box, and wondered, while daydreaming, what would happen to it if she happened to die.
In the first few days, she occupied herself with contemplating changes in her house.

She removed the globes from the candlesticks, had new wallpaper put up, repainted the staircase, and had benches made in the garden all around the sundial; she even asked how to go about having a water fountain with fish.
Finally, her husband, knowing that she enjoyed going out in a carriage, found a second-hand cab that, with once new lanterns and leather splash guards, almost resembled a tilbury.

sentences: Now that this resolution was made, it remained to carry it out.
It was only after a long search that Passepartout discovered a local antique dealer, to whom he presented his request.
The European outfit pleased the dealer, and soon Passepartout emerged dressed in an old Japanese robe and wearing a sort of ribbed turban, faded by the passage of time.
But in return, a few coins jingled in his pocket.
"Well, he thought, I'll pretend that we're at carnival!"

Passepartout's first concern, thus 'Japanese-ified', was to enter a modest-looking tea house, where he had lunch with some leftover poultry and a few handfuls of rice, as a man for whom dinner would still be a problem to solve.
"Now, he said to himself when he was well-restored, I must not lose my head.
I no longer have the option of selling this outfit for another one that's even more Japanese.
Therefore, I must find a way to leave this land of the Sun as quickly as possible, of which I will keep only a lamentable memory!"
Passepartout then thought about visiting the ships departing for America.
He intended to offer himself as a cook or a servant, asking for nothing in return except passage and food.
Once in San Francisco, he would figure out how to manage.
The important thing was to cross the four thousand seven hundred miles of the Pacific that stretch between Japan and the New World.
Passepartout, not being the kind of man to let an idea linger, headed towards the port of Yokohama.
But as he got closer to the docks, his plan, which had seemed so simple when he first thought of it, appeared increasingly unfeasible.
Why would anyone need a cook or a servant on board an American ship, and what trust would he inspire, dressed like that?
What recommendations should he present?
What references should he provide?

sentences: As a child, little Vampa had a strange character.
One day, at the age of seven, he went to see the priest of Palestrina and asked him to teach him to read.
It was a difficult task; for the young shepherd could not leave his flock.
But the good priest went every day to say mass in a poor little village too insignificant to pay a priest, and which, not even having a name, was known as dell'Borgo.
He offered Luigi to meet him on his way back and give him his lesson, warning him that this lesson would be short and that he should therefore make the most of it.
The child accepted joyfully.

Every day, Luigi led his flock to graze on the road from Palestrina to Borgo; every day, at nine in the morning, the priest passed by, and the priest and the child would sit on the edge of a ditch, and the little shepherd would take his lesson from the priest's breviary.
After three months, he could read.
That wasn't all; he now needed to learn to write.

The priest had a writing teacher from Rome make three alphabets for him: one in large, one in medium, and one in small, and he showed him that by following this alphabet on a slate, he could learn to write with the help of a metal point.

That same evening, when the flock was brought back to the farm, little Vampa ran to the blacksmith of Palestrina, took a large nail, forged it, hammered it, rounded it, and made it into a kind of ancient stylus.
The next day, he had gathered a supply of slates and set to work.
After three months, he could write.
The priest, astonished by this profound intelligence and touched by this ability, gifted him several notebooks, a packet of pens, and a penknife.
It was a new study to undertake, but one that was nothing compared to the first.
Eight days later, he handled the pen as skillfully as he handled the stylus.

The priest recounted this anecdote to the Count of San-Felice, who wanted to see the little shepherd, had him read and write in front of him, ordered his steward to have him eat with the servants, and gave him two piastres a month.

sentences: Indeed, the storm could be heard howling around the house.
The snow that was falling, almost solidified already, crackled against the frost on the windows.
High-pitched whistles, passing through the joints of the doors and windows, sometimes rose to the limit of audible sounds.
Then, a great silence fell.
Nature seemed to catch its breath, and once again, the gust unleashed itself with terrible force.
You could feel the house trembling on its stilts, the boards creaking, the beams groaning.
A stranger, less accustomed than the fort's inhabitants to these atmospheric convulsions, would have wondered if the storm was going to carry away this assembly of planks and beams.
But Captain Craventy's guests were little concerned about the gust, and even outside, they would not have been more frightened than those little devils playing in the midst of the storms.
However, regarding these guests, a few observations need to be made.
The gathering included about a hundred individuals of both sexes; but only two -- two women -- did not belong to the usual staff of Fort-Reliance.
This staff consisted of Captain Craventy, Lieutenant Jasper Hobson, Sergeant Long, Corporal Joliffe, and about sixty soldiers or employees of the Company.

Some of them were married, including Corporal Joliffe, a happy husband of a lively and alert Canadian woman, a certain Mac Nap, a Scot married to a Scottish woman, and John Raë, who had recently taken a wife among the local Indian women.
All these people, regardless of rank, officers, employees, or soldiers, were being entertained that evening by Captain Craventy.
It should be added here that the Company's staff did not provide its contingent to the party alone.
The nearby forts -- and in these remote areas, one is neighbors at a hundred miles distance -- had accepted Captain Craventy's invitation.
Many employees or factors had come from Fort Providence or Fort Resolution, which belonged to the Slave Lake district, and even from Fort Chipewan and Fort Liard located further south.
It was a rare entertainment, an unexpected distraction that these recluses, these exiles, who were half lost in the solitude of the hyperborean regions, eagerly sought.

sentences: Observe the scene, so mundane that it goes unnoticed: two strangers meet, and after the name comes almost always the same question — 'and what do you do for a living?'
We respond with our profession, as if it were obvious that employment summarizes our being.
'I am a doctor,' 'I am a teacher,' 'I am unemployed': the formula is revealing.
We don't say 'I work as,' we say 'I am.'
The profession is not presented as an activity, but as an identity.
This linguistic habit says a lot about the place that work has taken in our lives.
That this place is significant is not absurd in itself.
Work occupies the largest part of our adult days; it structures time, provides income, and connects people.
A job that has meaning, where one feels useful and competent, is one of the most solid sources of satisfaction.
No one seriously dreams of a life of total idleness: prolonged boredom is a torment, and many retirees discover this with surprise.
Wanting to banish work from our lives would be as futile as it is naive.
The problem is not work itself, but its excessive grip on the idea we have of ourselves.
Reducing a person to their job is to amputate everything else.
We are also parents, friends, neighbors, music or mountain lovers, curious individuals, citizens, and dreamers.
None of this appears in a job title.
A human being infinitely exceeds their role, and forgetting this impoverishes first and foremost the one who forgets it about themselves.
This confusion has a cost, which is cruelly revealed at certain turning points.
What does someone feel who loses their job if their job was their identity?
They lose not only an income, but the ground beneath their feet, the very feeling of existing.
And what do so many people discover at retirement, after a life completely devoted to work?
That they have neglected friendships, passions, family life — everything that was supposed to 'wait', and which did not wait.
They find themselves rich in time but poor in everything else.
The cult of work sometimes presents its bill very late, and it is heavy.
This is not about preaching disengagement or despising ambition, which has its nobility.
It is about not confusing a part with the whole.
Work is a part of life; it should not consume the others, nor claim a monopoly on meaning and dignity.
Perhaps we should, to begin with, change our questions.
Instead of asking a stranger, 'What do you do?', we could ask, 'What are you passionate about?', 'How are you?'.
We would discover people, where we previously only gathered functions.
And we would remember, by the way, that we are not what we do to earn a living.
We are what we do with our lives.

sentences: These sad doctrines, now applauded at public meetings, have lost this man.

It's not him that should be condemned, gentlemen, it's the Commune!
Murmurs of approval ran through the crowd.
It was clear that the case was won for the lawyer.
The public prosecutor did not reply.
Then the president asked the defendant the customary question:
--Defendant, do you have anything to add in your defense?
The man stood up:
He was short, with flaxen hair, and had gray, fixed, and clear eyes.
A strong, frank, and resonant voice came from this frail boy and suddenly changed, with the first words, the opinion that had been formed of him.
He spoke loudly, in a declamatory tone, but so clearly that his slightest words could be heard all the way to the back of the large hall:
Mr. President, since I don't want to go to an insane asylum, and I would even prefer the guillotine, I'm going to tell you everything.

sentences: The priest wiped his fingers, threw the oil-soaked cotton into the fire, and returned to sit beside the dying woman to tell her that she should now join her sufferings to those of Jesus Christ and surrender to divine mercy.
As he finished his exhortations, he tried to place a blessed candle in her hand, a symbol of the heavenly glories that she would soon be surrounded by.
But Emma, too weak, could not close her fingers, and the candle would have fallen to the ground without Mr. Bournisien.
However, she was no longer as pale, and her face had an expression of serenity, as if the sacrament had healed her.

The priest did not fail to point this out; he even explained to Bovary that the Lord sometimes prolonged the lives of people when He deemed it appropriate for their salvation; and Charles remembered a day when, being so close to death, she had received communion.
Perhaps there was no need to despair, he thought.

Indeed, she looked around her slowly, like someone waking from a dream, then, in a distinct voice, she asked for her mirror, and she leaned over it for some time, until large tears streamed down her cheeks.
Then she tilted her head back with a sigh and fell back onto the pillow.
Her chest immediately began to heave rapidly.

Her entire tongue stuck out of her mouth; her eyes, rolling, were growing pale like two lamp globes that are going out—leading one to believe she was already dead, were it not for the terrifying acceleration of her ribs shaken by a furious breath, as if her soul were making leaps to detach itself.
Félicité knelt before the crucifix, and the pharmacist himself slightly bent his knees, while Mr. Canivet looked vaguely around the square.
Bournisien had resumed his prayers, his face inclined against the edge of the bed, with his long black cassock trailing behind him in the room.
Charles was on the other side, kneeling, his arms outstretched toward her.
He had taken her hands and was holding them tightly, trembling with each beat of his heart, like the aftershock of a collapsing ruin.

And as the rattle grew louder, the clergyman hastened his prayers; they mingled with Bovary's stifled sobs, and sometimes everything seemed to fade into the muffled murmur of the Latin syllables, which rang out like the tolling of a bell.

sentences: Valentine saw him and showed no surprise.
There are no more intermediate emotions in a heart swollen by supreme despair.
Morrel reached out his hand to his friend.
Valentine, as an excuse for not having gone to find him, showed him the corpse lying under the funeral cloth and began to sob again.
Neither of them dared to speak in that room.
Everyone hesitated to break the silence that seemed to be commanded by Death standing in some corner with a finger on its lips.
Finally, Valentine was the first to dare.
"Friend," she said, "how did you get here?
Alas! I would say to you: welcome, if it weren't for Death who had opened the door to this house for you.

My friends, we have only two options: either risk our lives to replenish the fuel supply, or gradually burn the benches, the beds, the partitions, everything in this house that can feed our stoves!
But this is a last resort, because the cold may last, and nothing suggests a change in the weather.

Sitting on a low chair near the fireplace, he was spinning the ivory case in his fingers; she was pushing her needle, or, from time to time, with her nail, she was creasing the folds of the fabric.
She wasn't speaking; he was silent, captivated by her silence, just as he would have been by her words.
Poor boy! she thought.

sentences: Come, come! I shouted, pulling my uncle, who for the first time let himself be led!
A quarter of an hour later, we were out of sight of that fearsome enemy.
And now that I think about it calmly, now that peace has returned to my mind, that months have passed since that strange and supernatural encounter, what to think, what to believe?
No! It's impossible!
Our senses have been deceived, our eyes did not see what they were seeing!
No human creature exists in this underground world!
No generation of men inhabits these lower caverns of the globe, without caring for the inhabitants of its surface, without communication with them!
It's insane, deeply insane!

I would rather admit the existence of some animal whose structure is similar to that of humans, some monkey from the earliest geological periods, some Protopithecus, some Mesopithecus like the one discovered by Mr. Lartet in the fossil site of Sansan!
But this one exceeded in size all the measurements given by paleontology!
It doesn't matter!
A monkey, yes, a monkey, however unlikely it may be!
But a man, a living man, and with him an entire generation buried in the depths of the earth!
Never!

sentences: But despite all that, Château-Renaud murmured, Albert isn't coming; he's ten minutes late.
Here he is, said Beauchamp, he's on horseback; look, he's coming at full speed followed by his servant.
What recklessness, said Château-Renaud, to come on horseback to fight a duel!
I had given him such a good lesson!

And then, look, said Beauchamp, with a collar on his tie, with an open coat, with a white waistcoat; why didn't he just have a fly drawn on his stomach right away? It would have been simpler and over sooner!
Meanwhile, Albert had arrived ten steps from the group formed by the five young men; he stopped his horse, jumped down, and handed the reins to his servant.
Albert approached.
He was pale, his eyes were red and swollen.
You could see that he hadn't slept a wink all night.
There was, spread across his whole face, a shade of sad seriousness that was unusual for him.
Thank you, gentlemen, he said, for having kindly accepted my invitation: believe me, I am extremely grateful to you for this gesture of friendship.

sentences: Goodbye! Goodbye, our poor polar home!" said Mrs. Paulina Barnett, waving her hand one last time.
And all of them, with this final memory, sadly and silently took the road back.
At one o'clock, the detachment had arrived at Cape Michel, after turning around the gap that the insufficient cold of winter had been unable to close.
Until then, the difficulties of the journey had not been great, as the ground of Victoria Island had a relatively even surface.
But it would be quite different on the ice field.

Indeed, the icefield, subjected to the enormous pressure of the northern pack ice, had undoubtedly become rugged with icebergs, hummocks, and frozen mountains, among which they would have to search incessantly for passable routes, at the cost of the greatest efforts and extreme fatigue.
By the evening of that day, they had advanced a few miles onto the ice field.
It was necessary to organize the sleeping arrangements.
To this end, they proceeded in the manner of the Eskimos and the Indians of northern America, digging 'snow houses' in the blocks of ice.

The snow knives worked effectively and skillfully, and at eight o'clock, after a dinner of dried meats, all the personnel of the trading post had slipped into these holes, which are warmer than one might be tempted to believe.

Thank you, said the young man.
--Oh! it's from the heart, Caderousse added, laughing his big laugh.
Wait, let me walk you out.
--It's not necessary.
--Yes, it is.

--Oh! because there's a little secret at the door; it's a precautionary measure that I thought I should adopt; Huret and Fichet lock, reviewed and corrected by Gaspard Caderousse.

sentences: Some of them, who had already arrived, were playing marbles on the slabs of the cemetery.
Others, straddling the wall, were swinging their legs, cutting down the tall nettles that grew between the small enclosure and the last graves.
It was the only place that was green; everything else was just stones, and it was constantly covered in a fine dust, despite the sacristy's broom.
The children in slippers ran around there as if it were a floor made for them, and their voices could be heard above the buzzing of the bell.
It diminished with the swaying of the thick rope that, falling from the heights of the bell tower, dragged on the ground by its end.
Swallows flew by, making little cries, slicing through the air with the sharpness of their flight, and quickly returned to their yellow nests under the tiles of the eaves.
At the back of the church, a lamp was burning, that is to say, a wick of a nightlight in a hanging glass.
From a distance, its light looked like a whitish spot that trembled on the oil.
A long ray of sunlight crossed the entire nave and made the side aisles and corners even darker.
— Where is the priest? asked Madame Bovary of a young boy who was having fun shaking the turnstile in its too-loose hole.
— He will come, he replied.
Indeed, the door of the presbytery creaked, Abbé Bournisien appeared; the children, in a jumble, fled into the church.
Those little rascals! murmured the clergyman, always the same!
And, picking up a torn catechism that he had just kicked with his foot:
It shows no respect for anything!

sentences: The notary backed out while bowing deeply; it was the first time, since the day he took his registrations, that he encountered such a client.
"Take him to his destination," said the count to Bertuccio.
And the steward followed the notary out.
As soon as the count was alone, he took a locked portfolio from his pocket, which he opened with a small key attached to his neck that he never parted with.
After searching for a moment, he stopped at a page that had some notes, compared those notes with the sales deed laid on the table, and, gathering his thoughts:
"Auteuil, rue de la Fontaine, no. 28; that's right," he said; "now should I rely on a confession obtained through religious terror or physical terror?
Besides, in an hour I will know everything.
Bertuccio! he shouted, striking a kind of small folding-handle hammer on a bell that produced a sharp and prolonged sound like that of a tam-tam, Bertuccio!"
The steward appeared in the doorway.
"Mr. Bertuccio," said the count, "didn't you once tell me that you had traveled in France?
--In certain parts of France, yes, Your Excellency.
--You know the surroundings of Paris, no doubt?
No, Your Excellency, no, replied the steward with a kind of nervous tremor that Monte-Cristo, an expert in emotions, rightly attributed to a deep anxiety.

It's unfortunate, he said, that you have never visited the outskirts of Paris, because I want to go see my new property this very evening, and by coming with me, you would undoubtedly have provided useful information.
To Auteuil? exclaimed Bertuccio, whose coppery complexion turned almost ashen.
Me, go to Auteuil!
Well then, what is so surprising about your coming to Auteuil, I ask you?
When I stay in Auteuil, you will have to come there, since you are part of the household.
Bertuccio lowered his head before the imperious gaze of his master, and he remained still and silent.
Ah! But what is happening to you?
Are you going to make me ring for the carriage a second time? said Monte-Cristo in the tone that Louis XIV used to say the famous, 'I almost waited!'
Bertuccio leaped from the small sitting room to the anteroom and shouted in a hoarse voice:

sentences: This burden that I have lifted, almost as heavy as a world, and which I thought I could carry to the end, was according to my desire and not according to my strength; according to my will and not according to my power, and I will have to lay it down barely halfway through my journey.
Oh! I will therefore become a fatalist again, I who have been made providential by fourteen years of despair and ten years of hope.

And all of this, my God! because my heart, which I thought was dead, was only numb; because it has awakened, because it has beaten, because I yielded to the pain of this beating stirred from the depths of my chest by the voice of a woman!

And yet, the count continued, sinking deeper into the predictions of that terrible tomorrow that Mercédès had accepted; yet it is impossible that this woman, who has such a noble heart, could have selfishly consented to let me be killed, I who am full of strength and life!
It is impossible that she loves to such an extent, or rather that she is in a maternal frenzy!
There are virtues whose exaggeration would be a crime.
No, she must have imagined some pathetic scene, she will come to throw herself between the swords, and it will be ridiculous on the ground, compared to the sublime it was here.
And the flush of pride rose to the count's forehead.
Ridiculous, he repeated, and the ridicule will rebound on me...
Me, ridiculous!
Come on! I would rather die.
And by constantly exaggerating in advance the bad chances of tomorrow, to which he had condemned himself by promising Mercédès to let her son live, the count came to tell himself:
Nonsense, nonsense, nonsense! What good is generosity if it is placed as an inert target at the end of this young man's pistol!
He will never believe that my death is a suicide, and yet it is important for the honor of my memory...

(This is not vanity, is it, my God? But rather a rightful pride, that's all), it is important for the honor of my memory that the world knows that I myself consented, of my own will, freely, to stop my arm already raised to strike, and that with this arm, so powerfully armed against others, I struck myself: it must be done, I will do it.

sentences: The police prefect's envoy presented his letter of introduction to Lord Wilmore.
He read it with all the composure of an Englishman; then, when he had finished reading:
"I understand," he said in English; "I understand very well."
Then the questioning began.
They were roughly the same as those that had been addressed to Abbé Busoni.

But since Lord Wilmore, in his capacity as an enemy of the Count of Monte Cristo, did not exercise the same restraint as the abbé, the questions were much more extensive; he recounted Monte Cristo's youth, which, according to him, began when he entered the service of one of those small Indian sovereigns who waged war against the English at the age of ten; it was there that he, Wilmore, had first encountered him, and they had fought against each other.
In that war, Zaccone had been captured, sent to England, placed on the hulks, from which he had escaped by swimming.
Then his travels, duels, and passions began; then the Greek insurrection occurred, and he served in the ranks of the Greeks.
While he was in their service, he discovered a silver mine in the mountains of Thessaly, but he was careful not to mention this discovery to anyone.
After Navarino, and when the Greek government was consolidated, he asked King Otto for a mining concession for this mine, and this concession was granted to him.
From there came this immense fortune, which, according to Lord Wilmore, could amount to one or two million in revenue, a fortune that could, however, suddenly dry up if the mine itself ran out.
"But," asked the visitor, "do you know why he came to France?"
He wants to speculate on railroads, said Lord Wilmore; and then, since he is a skilled chemist and no less distinguished physicist, he has discovered a new telegraph that he is working on.
How much does he spend approximately per year? asked the envoy of the Prefect of Police.
Oh! five or six hundred thousand francs, at most, said Lord Wilmore; he is stingy.
It was clear that hatred was driving the Englishman to speak, and that, not knowing what to accuse the count of, he was blaming him for his stinginess.

sentences: Then you will be known to be abandoned, and people will believe you are poor; for I alone know your financial situation and am ready to give you my accounts as a loyal partner.
The baroness, pale and horrified, listened to this speech with as much dread and despair as Debray had shown calmness and indifference in delivering it.
Abandoned! she repeated, oh! very abandoned...
Yes, you are right, sir, and no one will doubt my abandonment.
These were the only words that this woman, so proud and so violently in love, could reply to Debray.
But rich, very rich indeed, Debray continued, pulling out some papers from his wallet and spreading them on the table.
Mrs. Danglars let him do this, completely occupied with stifling the beats of her heart and holding back the tears that she felt welling up at the edge of her eyelids.
But finally, the feeling of dignity prevailed in the baroness; and although she did not succeed in suppressing her heart, she at least managed not to shed a tear.
Madam, Debray said, it has been about six months since we became partners.
You provided an initial investment of one hundred thousand francs.
It was in April of this year that our partnership took place.
In May, our operations began.
In May, we earned four hundred and fifty thousand francs.
In June, the profit rose to nine hundred thousand.
In July, we added one million seven hundred thousand francs; as you know, it's the month of Spanish bonds.

In August, we lost three hundred thousand francs at the beginning of the month; but by the 15th, we had made up for it, and by the end, we had taken our revenge; for our accounts, settled from the day of our partnership until yesterday when I closed them, show us an asset of two million four hundred thousand francs, which means twelve hundred thousand francs for each of us.
Now, Debray continued, consulting his notebook with the methodical calm of a stockbroker, we find eighty thousand francs for the compound interest on this sum that has remained in my hands.
--But, interrupted the baroness, what do these interests mean, since you have never put this money to use?

sentences: He was no longer the same man, and five minutes had been enough to bring about a sad transformation in Albert; he had left in his usual state, and he was returning with a changed voice, a face marked by feverish redness, eyes sparkling beneath blue-veined eyelids, and a staggering gait like that of a drunk man.
"Count," he said, "thank you for your kind hospitality, which I would have liked to enjoy longer, but I must return to Paris.
--What has happened?
--A great misfortune; but please allow me to leave, it concerns something far more precious than my life.
No questions, count, I beg you, just a horse!
--My stables are at your service, viscount," said Monte-Cristo; "but you will exhaust yourself with fatigue running to the post on horseback; take a carriage, a cab, some vehicle.
--No, that would take too long, and besides, I need this fatigue that you fear for me; it will do me good."
Albert took a few steps, swaying like a man struck by a bullet, and fell into a chair near the door.
Monte-Cristo did not see this second weakness; he was at the window, shouting:
"Ali, a horse for Mr. de Morcerf! Hurry up! He is in a hurry!"
These words revived Albert; he dashed out of the room, and the count followed him.
Thank you! murmured the young man as he jumped into the saddle.
You will return as quickly as you can, Florentin.
Is there a password for me to get some horses?
--None other than to return the one you are riding; another one will be saddled for you right away.
Albert was about to leap forward, but he stopped.
You may find my departure strange, foolish, said the young man.

You don't understand how a few lines written in a newspaper can drive a man to despair; well, he added, throwing the newspaper at him, read this, but only after I have left, so you don't see my embarrassment.

And while the count picked up the newspaper, he dug the spurs, which had just been attached to his boots, into the horse's belly, which, surprised that there was a rider who believed he needed such a stimulant, took off like a bolt from a crossbow.

sentences: During the first act, Countess G... entered her box; her first glance was directed towards the spot where she had seen the Count the day before, so she caught sight of Franz and Albert in the box of the man about whom she had expressed such a strange opinion to Franz twenty-four hours earlier.

Her lorgnette was aimed at him with such intensity that Franz realized it would be cruel to delay any longer in satisfying her curiosity; thus, taking advantage of the privilege granted to spectators in Italian theaters, which allows them to treat the performance halls as their reception rooms, the two friends left their box to pay their respects to the Countess.
Hardly had they entered her box when she signaled for Franz to take the place of honor.
Albert, in turn, positioned himself behind.
"Well," she said, barely giving Franz time to sit down, "it seems you couldn't wait to get acquainted with the new Lord Ruthwen, and now you’re the best of friends?"
"While we’re not as far along in mutual intimacy as you suggest, I cannot deny, Madame Countess," replied Franz, "that we have taken advantage of his kindness all day long."
"What, all day long?"

"Indeed, that’s the word: this morning we accepted his invitation for lunch, during the entire mascherata we drove around the Corso in his carriage, and finally, this evening we came to the theater in his box."
"So you know him then?"
"Yes and no."
"How so?"
"It's a long story."
What will you tell me?
It would scare you too much.
All the more reason.
At least wait until this story has a conclusion.
Fine, I like complete stories.
In the meantime, how did you come into contact? Who introduced you to him?
No one; it was he, on the contrary, who had himself introduced to us.
When was that?
Last night, when I was leaving you.
By what means?
Oh! my God! by the very prosaic means of our host!
So he is staying at the Hotel d'Espagne, like you?
Not only in the same hotel, but on the same square.

sentences: On Wednesday afternoon, it was raining heavily.
My son Léo was watching the rain through the window, a bit disappointed: no football today.
Suddenly, he asked me: "Dad, where does all this water come from?"
I proposed a deal to him: I'll explain it to you, and then we'll make pancakes.
The story of rain is a great journey.
It starts far from here, at the sea.
The sun heats the water of the sea, lakes, and rivers.
When the water gets hot, some of it rises into the air, invisible.
This invisible water is called steam.
"Like above the pot?" Léo asked.
Exactly!
The steam rises high into the sky.
Up there, it is cold.
Then the steam transforms into tiny drops.
Millions of drops gather and form...
"A cloud!" shouted Léo.
Well done!
The wind pushes the clouds over the cities and mountains.
The drops grow larger, the cloud becomes gray and heavy.
And when it is too heavy, the drops fall.
It's rain.
Then, rainwater enters the ground, finds the rivers, and the rivers return to the sea.
And everything starts again!
This journey is called the water cycle.
Léo looked at the rain with new eyes.
So, rain is the sea that travels.
And now, the pancakes.
I promise, it's a promise.

sentences: A year ago, I downloaded an app and wrote in my notebook: "Goal: speak Spanish."
Why Spanish?
A dream of traveling to Andalusia, and a colleague from Madrid, Carmen.
The beginning was a lesson in humility.
In the first weeks, I mixed everything up.
I said "I am tired" instead of "I am happy."
One evening in November, feeling discouraged, I almost gave up.
It was Carmen who saved me, with a simple piece of advice: "Stop the long sessions on Sundays.
Do ten minutes a day."
She was right.
A year later, I have hardly ever missed a day.
I also found my own methods.
I listen to Spanish songs and I look for the lyrics.
I watch cartoons: they speak slowly, it's perfect.
And on Fridays, Carmen and I only speak in Spanish.
And then, in May, the trip.
Seville, at last.
In a café, I ordered in Spanish, talked with the waiter about football, understood his jokes.
When leaving, I had a huge smile.
I still make a lot of mistakes.
Last week, I told Carmen that I had "eaten a door" instead of a soup.
She still laughs about it.
But mistakes are not the enemy.
Silence, yes.
Year two: goal Andalusia, long version.
And maybe, after that, Italian?

sentences: Eat local!
The advice is everywhere: at markets, in magazines, and from politicians.
The idea seems to be based on common sense: food that travels less pollutes less.
Buying tomatoes from the local producer instead of those that travel across Europe by truck obviously seems more ecological.
And yet, the reality is more subtle — and more interesting.
Let's start with what is true.
The short supply chain has undeniable advantages.
It supports local farmers, who receive a fairer share of the price.
It guarantees fresher products, picked riper, and often better.
It keeps rural areas vibrant and preserves local know-how.
These reasons are more than enough to support the Saturday market.
But when it comes to the climate, things get complicated.
Because transport, contrary to what we believe, only accounts for a small part of the carbon footprint of our food — often less than ten percent.
The key issue lies elsewhere: in the way we produce.
A striking example: the tomato.
A tomato grown next to you, but in the middle of winter in a gas-heated greenhouse, can emit several times more carbon than a tomato from Spain grown under the simple sun and transported by truck.
The journey of a thousand kilometers weighs less than the heating of the greenhouse.
So 'local' does not automatically mean 'clean': it all depends on the season and the method.

Similarly, a lamb raised outdoors on the other side of the world and arriving by boat — the most economical mode of transport — can compete, in carbon footprint, with meat produced intensively nearby.
The boat carries tons of goods for very little emissions per kilo.
It's the airplane that is disastrous: so be cautious with fragile and exotic products that travel by air.
What can we take away from all this, concretely?
First of all, the season matters more than the distance.
The most accurate reasoning can be summed up in one formula: local AND in season.
June strawberries from your region, yes; January strawberries, no — whether they come from far away or from a nearby greenhouse.
Next, the contents of the plate weigh more than its origin.
Reducing meat a little has more of an effect on the climate than any hunt for food miles.
Eating local is still a great idea — for the taste, for the producers, for the joy of the market.
You just need to add a calendar to it.

sentences: Eating healthily is complicated and expensive.
This idea is very common, but it is false.
In reality, eating well is based on a few simple habits, and it gives the body the energy it needs.
The first rule is easy: eat more vegetables and fruits.
They are full of vitamins, they are inexpensive, especially when in season, and they fill you up without tiring the body.
In every meal, half of the plate should be vegetables.
The second rule concerns sugar.
Today, we eat way too much sugar, often without realizing it: in sodas, cakes, but also in products that don't taste sweet.
Sugar provides a quick energy boost, then a big fatigue an hour later.
It's better to avoid it and drink water.
The third rule is perhaps the most important: cook for yourself.
When you prepare your own meal, you know what you're eating.
You don't need to be a great chef: a soup, a salad, a pasta dish with vegetables, it's simple and balanced.
Eating healthily doesn't mean depriving yourself of everything.
You can treat yourself from time to time.
What's important is the daily habit.
The body, like a car, works better with good fuel.

I really enjoy these mornings.
The children play with a lot of energy and little organization.
They all run towards the ball at the same time.
But there is a problem on the edge of the field: some parents shout too much.
One father, in particular, is constantly shouting at his son: "Pass!"
Run!
But what are you doing?"
The boy is eight years old and he lowers his head every time.

He turned to the parents and said calmly:

There was a great silence.
After that, the match continued, and it was much more enjoyable.
Léo scored a goal.
