sentences: Do what you love, and you will never work a single day in your life.
This saying, repeated a thousand times, summarizes a dominant demand: work should not only provide for us, but also inspire passion; we should love our job, thrive in it, and find self-fulfillment.
This injunction presents itself as a liberation, a step forward from the time when people worked without joy, purely out of necessity.
However, it must be examined closely, for beneath its benevolent appearance, the demand to love one's work may well conceal a trap.
Let’s first acknowledge what this aspiration has of legitimacy.
That one refuses to spend their life on a hated task, seeks something more than a salary in work, and aspires to an activity that has meaning and brings joy is nothing but healthy.
The idea that work could be loved, and not just endured, has freed many lives from resignation, and it would be absurd to condemn it outright.
The problem lies not in the aspiration to love one's work, but in its transformation into a norm, a duty, a general injunction.
Because as soon as love for work becomes a requirement, it turns against you.
First, it induces guilt.

Those who do not love their job — and there are many, as not all jobs are lovable — are made to feel that they have failed, that they have not found their path, and that their dissatisfaction is their fault.
Along with the pain of unloved work comes the shame of not loving it, as if it were a personal flaw.
The pressure to be professionally happy thus creates additional suffering for those who cannot meet it, which is to say, for most people.
Then, and above all, the demand to love your job serves a logic that is not innocent.

For someone who loves their job, they dedicate more to it, without counting the cost, without demanding anything in return; they accept conditions they would refuse for a job that is merely a means to an end; they confuse their personal fulfillment with the interests of their employer.
The demand for passion can thus become a powerful tool for exploitation, which, in the name of love for the profession, secures unlimited commitment and often without fair compensation.
"Do what you love" can practically mean: "Since you love it, you won’t count your hours and won’t ask for what you’re owed."
The sectors that demand the most passion are often those that pay the least.
There’s more.
The ideology of loving work assumes that everyone could find a job they are passionate about, as if such jobs existed in sufficient numbers for everyone.
However, the vast majority of tasks necessary for collective life are not exciting, and someone will have to carry them out.
To claim that everyone should love their work is to ignore the reality of these essential and thankless tasks, and to place the burden of an unattainable ideal on those who perform them.
This is a discourse of the privileged, projecting a possibility onto everyone that is reserved for a few.
Perhaps we should therefore free work from this very injunction.

Not to return to the resignation of the past, but to give work a more just place: an activity that can be loved, but does not have to be; that can have meaning, without requiring it to fulfill all of existence.

One can do a job properly, and without shame, even if they are not passionately in love with it, by finding elsewhere — in their relationships, their passions, their life outside of work — what allows them to thrive.
This more modest conception is also freer: it frees one from the guilt of not loving, and from the exploitation that hides under the demanded love.
Loving one’s work, when it happens, is a chance; making it a duty is a way to bind ourselves even more closely to it — at the risk of having no life outside of it to love.

sentences: I was called three months ago to the bedside of that old woman.
She had arrived the day before in the vehicle that served as her home, pulled by the nag you saw, and accompanied by her two large black dogs, her friends and guardians.
The priest was already there.
She made us her executors, and to reveal the meaning of her last wishes, she told us her whole life story.
I know nothing more singular and more poignant.
Her father was a chair caner and her mother a chair caner.
She never had a home rooted in the ground.
When she was very little, she wandered around, ragged, infested, and squalid.

They would stop at the entrance of the villages, along the ditches; they would unhitch the cart; the horse would graze; the dog slept, its muzzle on its paws; and the little girl rolled in the grass while her father and mother repaired, in the shade of the roadside elms, all the old seats of the community.
There was hardly any conversation in that mobile home.
After the few necessary words to decide who would go around the houses shouting the well-known cry: 'Chair caner!', they would start twisting straw, face to face or side by side.
When the child wandered too far or tried to engage with some village urchin, her father's angry voice would call her back: 'Will you come back here, you little rascal!'
Those were the only words of affection she heard.
When she got older, she was sent to collect the scraps of damaged seats.

Then she began to make a few acquaintances from place to place with the kids; but it was then the parents of her new friends who would harshly call their children back: 'Will you come here, you little scamp!'
‘I want to see you talking to the beggars!...’

Polyte was not far from a meter.
The door opened.
Mélie appeared, and right away, before she had even said hello to us: "... You dirty pigs, you both had the meter."
Then Mathieu got angry: "Don't say that, Mélie, don't say that, I've never been to the meter."
We were served an exquisite lunch, in front of the door, under two linden trees, next to the little chapel of "Our Lady of the Big Belly" and facing the immense landscape.
And Mathieu told us, with a mix of mockery and unexpected credulity, unbelievable stories of miracles.

We had drunk a lot of that lovely, tangy, sweet, fresh, and intoxicating cider that he preferred to all other drinks; and we were smoking our pipes, perched on our chairs, when two old women showed up.
They were old, thin, and bent.
After greeting us, they asked for Saint Blanc.
Mathieu winked at us and replied:
--I'll get that for you.
And he disappeared into his woodpile.
He stayed there for a good five minutes; then he came back looking distraught.
He raised his arms:
--I don't know where he is, I can't find him; I'm sure I had him.
Then, using his hands as a megaphone, he called out again: "Mélie-e-e!"
From the back of the yard, his wife replied:
--"What's wrong?"
--"Where is Saint Blanc?
I can't find him in the woodpile."
Then, Mélie offered this explanation:
--"Isn't he the one you took last week to plug the hole in the rabbit hutch?"
